This desire for diversification on a portfolio results in a minimization problem where the portfolio's asset allocation vector is optimized to resemble a standard stock market structure as closely as possible, while also remaining unique.  This minimization problem can be reimagined as an optimization task that seeks to maximize a measure of standard market structure and minimize a replication cost, essentially transforming it into an optimization task of finding a local maximum in a space where the portfolio's asset allocation vector diverges from the standard market structure as little or as much as possible.  Recent advancements in generative adversarial networks have enabled the exploration of new methods in exploring this space by generating samples from a learned standard market structure distribution. The system achieves this by incorporating an autoencoding component that removes noise from the standard market structure and reassembling it to produce a diverse set of portfolios when combined with the conditional generative adversarial network component. In recent years, the use of cubic splines in the treatment evaluation of diseases such as Alzheimer's has become more prevalent. Cubic splines offer a flexible framework for modeling, but their interpretation can be complex. This study seeks to elucidate the application of a specific type of modeling approach, natural cubic splines, by applying it to the evaluation of treatments for Alzheimer's. We utilize data from the BANZAI trial, a placebo-controlled study examining minocycline as a preventive treatment, and compare its findings to those from a previous analysis. We demonstrate that with a well-explained variable and an adequate penalty, models employing natural cubic splines can significantly enhance understanding of the treatment's progressive effects and their timing, while also facilitating the interpretation of results in relation to specific time points, even without introducing additional parameters. This type of model is particularly useful for examining continuous endpoints like dementia ratings in Alzheimer's treatment evaluations. Additionally, with a properly implemented model, the effects of treatment can be accurately interpreted at time points other than those for which data is available. Finally, the utility of natural cubic splines in supporting model checking is discussed, including the implementation of diagnostics for continuous time models. Furthermore, our method allows robots to adapt dynamically to changes in their environment and to learn from one another when interacting with each other. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of numerical simulations and find that it results in a significant reduction of risk and journey time comparisons. Ultimately, this research is verified through real-world experiments. The obtained results showcase the ability of our model to successfully navigate and learn in complex robotic systems. As a result, this approach has the potential to be adopted widely in various applications where information theory plays a crucial role. It is particularly suitable for use in scenarios where there is a high likelihood of changes in the robot's surroundings. Such scenarios include package and package transport, as well as other related applications in logistics, for example the delivery service robots. In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal orthogonal waveforms, which assign unique sequences to users via joint sequence detection. This paper addresses two key issues with currently employed orthogonal sequences: the need for a higher throughput ratio of granted users and the vulnerability to sequence sequence correlation attacks. To address these problems, a new approach called the two-stage genetic algorithm (TGA) is proposed. First, the TGA seeks to optimize the throughput of granted users by identifying the most effective sequence selection. Next, the TGA places the selected sequences in subgroups to minimize the inter-group sequence correlation. This results in improved sequence diversity and a lower risk of sequence correlation. Our simulations show that the proposed TGA sequences yield a higher bit-error rate performance gain of 2.43 dB and a 43% increased throughput ratio of granted users compared to genetic algorithm (GA) sequences, as well as reduced sequence correlation. Additionally, the TGA sequences yield a performance gain of 0.57 dB with four antennas per device, a 57% increased throughput ratio of granted users, and reduced sequence correlation, compared to conventional orthogonal sequences. Furthermore, the TGA sequences perform well in the presence of multiple access interference (MAI) and are resistant to sequence correlation attacks. As a result, the required signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to achieve a bit error rate (BER) of 10^-3 is lower by 2.9 and 1.1 dB for 4 and 16 antennas per device, respectively. Finally, the TGA sequences perform well in a massive connectivity scenario and significantly reduce the required SNR to achieve a BER of 10^-3, by 2.9, 9.4, and 13.4 dB for 32, 64, and 128 antennas per device, respectively. This is because the TGA sequences minimize the inter-group sequence correlation, thus reducing the required SNR to detect the granted users' signals in the multi-user detection (MUD) process. As a result, the TGA achieves a performance gain in the MAI interference detection process and significantly reduces the required SNR to achieve a BER of 10^-3. Moreover, the TGA achieves a performance gain in sequence diversity, which reduces the probability of sequence correlation attacks. This is because the TGA groups the selected sequences to minimize the inter-group sequence correlation, thus improving the sequence diversity and reducing the probability of sequence correlation attacks.

The world's first commercial fusion reactors will likely adopt the tokamak design, specifically the Super-Stellaran tokamak proposed by Miller et al., which has shown that frequent pulse duration of just a few seconds is sufficient to achieve fusion activation. Nevertheless, tokamaks have exhibited so-called Palm Tree Modes during numerous experiments at the JET, C-Mod, and ASTRE, leading some to speculate that these phenomena might compromise fusion performance. This study reveals, however, that these modes do not in fact affect the outcome of fusion experiments. Moreover, the paper offers an explanation for the origins and significance of Palm Tree Modes, namely that they result from a non-resonant interaction between the edge of plasma and the magnetic field surrounding the vessel, a phenomenon that is not related to fusion. This realization allows researchers to separate the formation of Palm Tree Modes from other edge plasma instability issues, including the scrape-off layer. As a result, the modes are no longer considered a major concern for fusion achievement, and in fact, the JET Scientific Centre has demonstrated a plasma confinement enhancing technique called NCDB. The researchers' findings further underscore the importance of distinguishing between fusion relevant edge plasma processes and other nonessential interactions. They primarily rely on GCCEOM, a computational tool designed to analyze and manage non-resonant plasma-magnetic field interactions. This study offers valuable insights for tokamak scientists, providing a solid understanding of Palm Tree Modes and facilitating the exploration of new edge plasma research avenues, as well as a cross-check of existing theories. The authors propose that these modes, which have long been observed in ASTRE, JET, and C-Mod, might be triggered by an error in magnetic coil positioning, a possibility that remains the subject of further investigation. The study also opens the door for tokamak improvement by suggesting that these modes, which have hindered tokamak performance in ASTRE, JET, and C-Mod, might be completely eliminated through adjustments to the magnetic field configuration. The authors propose the adoption of a new tokamak configuration, the "Star-burst," which is designed to prevent Palm Tree Modes from arising. The study is a valuable resource for tokamak researchers, providing a clear and concise overview of Palm Tree Modes, which can serve as a springboard for exploring related topics, including edge plasma research, the scrape-off layer, and non-resonant plasma-magnetic field interactions. The authors' expertise in magnetic confinement fusion and plasma science informs this study, which can serve as a starting point for future research on Palm Tree Modes

The goal of Continual Learning (CL) is to develop models and algorithms capable of learning from multiple tasks over time. To date, the most effective CL methods have leveraged Pre-Training (PT) on a general knowledge base with subsequent Specialized Training (ST) on each individual task. However, this approach is reminiscent of utilizing a general-purpose tool to tackle every CL challenge. They also highlight the need for CL researchers to move beyond applying generic PT frameworks to new scenarios. This could potentially lead to a divergence in research directions that is unproductive. Identifying key components that drive the behavior of dense nuclear matter in different states is a primary objective for researchers. This goal spans from creating new heavy ions to analyzing how nuclear matter transforms at high densities. An alternative approach involves analyzing how individual nucleons interact within this matter. Ultimately, understanding the properties of quark-gluon matter at high temperatures and densities may hold the key to explaining the nature of strange heavy atomic nuclei and other peculiar phenomena. We propose a theoretical approach, analyzing 3D flow, to explore how nuclear matter behaves in distinct states. This method relies on a comprehensive analysis of the flow created by individual nucleons and collective effects during collisions. We have discovered significant parallels between 3d flow and other established instruments, such as the nuclear equation and the phasis diagram. Furthermore, 3d flow appears to be closely linked to the presence of collective effects in dense matter and the emergence of a specific state that may signal a phase transition. Additionally, collective effects seem to be less prominent in cases involving tiny nuclei at low energies. Overall, 3d flow presents an innovative and novel means for studying dense matter and detecting phases within it. Studying 3d flow also offers further opportunities to gain insights into the properties of dense matter created in high-energy collisions and to explore unexplored areas in this field. We suggest developing a dedicated experimental campaign to investigate this phenomenon using a chain of existing measurements. Utilizing heavy-ion collisions at low energies, this approach can yield valuable insights into the equation of state for dense matter at low temperatures and densities. Similar campaigns focused on examining 3d flow in experiments using light and intermediate nuclei at intermediate energies are feasible. They enable researchers to gain a more detailed understanding of dense matter created in high-energy collisions at the QCD critical point and to gain precious knowledge of the equation of state for such matter. Studying 3d flow also offers significant implications for understanding the transformation of dense matter at high densities. For example, this method can provide significant insights into the properties of quark-gluon plasma at high temperatures and to explore the possibility that the critical slope of dense matter could be an indicator of a phase transition. However, further theoretical research is required to establish the connection between 3d flow measurements and the phases of dense matter and to develop guidelines for detecting potential phases using 3d flow measurements. Researchers should also develop a dedicated experimental campaign to investigate this phenomenon using a combination of existing and new measurements. Ultimately, 3, flow presents an innovative and promising means for studying dense matter

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), characterized by their graph structure input/outputs and message passing mechanisms, are ideal for processing graph data. GNNs' graph structure is aligned with communication networks, making them a great fit. However, in wireless transmission systems, neural networks are typically applied point-to-point or in a centralized manner, neglecting the benefits of Graph Neural Networks. This study introduces a GNN-based approach to distributed inference in wireless transmission systems. To facilitate this, a wireless communication graph is defined along with a GNN model, followed by an exploration of two message passing mechanisms: (1) amplitude scaling to analyze the network's channel state information and (2) a novel phase scaling mechanism to outperform the amplitude scaling. The research also incorporates an iterative deep learning strategy to overcome noisy disturbances. The simulations confirm that the phase scaling approach offers enhanced performance over amplitude scaling and achieves near-ideal performance when dealing with noisy inputs. Additionally, the results reveal that the deep learning strategy can significantly improve the network's output when confronted with noisy channel state information. Ultimately, the research achieves a remarkable bit error rate performance, specifically an error rate of $10^{-4}$ for a large graph with 160 nodes. This achievement brings GNN-based solutions close to current state-of-the-art wireless transmission systems, opening the door to applying GNNs in next-generation wireless communication systems. The research hopes to motivate more widespread adoption of GNNs in wireless communication. The study's outcomes can guide future design in this area, specifically in introducing a variety of graph structure design strategies to support neural network-based inference. The research also brings together the benefits of both wireless communication systems and the graph structure benefits of GNNs, a combination previously overlooked. The study introduces a unique control mechanism: phase scaling, which contributes to the body of literature exploring various neural network-based message passing mechanisms. The research's outcome introduces a promising direction for future design: combining neural networks and the graph structure of communication graphs. The method, comprising a modified acquisition phase characterized by prolonged total acquisition time (T$_A$) and a correction phase involving image reconstruction and motion correction, effectively addresses breathing-related distortions. This proposed technique enables high-quality, distortion-free T2-weighted MRI scans without the need for compression or complex data processing. The method demonstrates generalizability across various acquisition parameters and sampling methods, while our research highlights the importance of considering respiratory distortions in the planning and analysis of body MRI scans. To improve efficiency, a smaller model (the student) needs to replicate the behavior of a larger model (the teacher) without relying on identical data inputs. Direct comparison using batch norms or other methods is not feasible. Therefore, we typically use layer-removed distillation to separate each layer of the teacher and extract the student's parameters through representative data. However, this approach has a significant drawback: it ignores how data interacts across different layers, leading to poor performance when using this distillation method for model compression. To address this challenge, we propose a model compression method called InDistill, which compresses a teacher model with batch norms by extracting a student model with batch norms. To achieve this, InDistill removes the effect of data flow, isolates each branch of batch norms, and reformulates the loss to preserve data flow. As a result, InDistill significantly improves the compression quality and maintains the compressed model's accuracy. Our model compression experiments show that InDistill achieves a top compression rate of 6.7x with minimal loss in test accuracy for various datasets and teacher models. Moreover, the source code for InDistill is available at https://github.com/zwang87/InDistill. InDistill achieved the first place in model compression track of 2022 NeurIPS Competition Congress and the first place in model compression track of 2022 ICCV Competition Congress. The topological similarity of these functions is defined by an homeomorphism between them and their respective critical sets, while the topological similarity of their foliations involves homeomorphisms that preserve orientation. It's demonstrated that for two linear-like functions with different configurations, the topological similarity of their foliations cannot extend beyond a $\varepsilon$-neighborhood for any $\varepsilon >0$. Additionally, for linear-like functions in a specific form, the topological similarity of their foliations cannot exceed a $\delta$-neighborhood for any $\delta >0$. The topological similarity of submersion functions and their foliations for all other cases can be extensively explored using new properties, with an exception of unique cases involving rotations of foliations whose proof has been postponed. The topological similarity of rotations for any $\varepsilon >0$ remains an issue to be addressed. The study of topological similarity of foliations for non-differentiable functions relies on the concept of continuous foliations. An extension to metric spaces has been explored. The outcomes of these investigations are significant in understanding the concept of topological similarity of foliations and its use in studying decision problems for special types of decision problems with rotational restrictions. It's demonstrated that for most cases, decision problems with these restrictions have a finite number of decision criteria. It's noted that the concept of rotational restriction might not be applicable in all cases, with an exception involving rotations of foliations whose proof has been postponed. The study of rotation values and its connection with topological similarity of foliations remains an issue to be addressed. The study has led to new challenges and questions in understanding the concept of topological similarity of foliations and its use in decision problems. However, no one study has accurately modeled this process or explored how it compares with real-world data. To fill this knowledge gap, researchers created a computational model that simulates the movement of grazing animals and its effects on the surrounding environment. By testing this model against actual data, researchers were able to develop an accurate mathematical relationship between plant growth and distance from an animal's residence area, showing that plants experience maximum growth within a specific range before declining as they move further away. These findings support the idea that constant grazing can lead to a decline in local vegetation cover. Interestingly, it takes relatively short periods of grazing (around 20 years) for this effect to occur, making overgrazing a pressing issue in so many dryland ecosystems worldwide. By identifying key parameters, researchers were able to explore various strategies to mitigate this issue. Ultimately, the study's findings highlight the intricate relationship between grazing patterns and the surrounding environment. By understanding this interaction, it may be possible to develop simple, straightforward solutions to mitigate overgrazing in dryland ecosystems. Furthermore, the study suggests a number of potential research directions that could help refine these solutions further. Specifically, future studies could help explore a number of potential factors that might influence overgrazing, such as the impact of other animals (like insects) on plant growth. By incorporating these additional elements, it may be possible to develop even more accurate models that can help us better understand this complex system. Such models could then be used to explore a number of pressing questions, such as the impact of climate change on plant growth in dryland ecosystems. Ultimately, the study's findings suggest a number of possibilities for future research that could help us better understand this complex system. We obtained a VETAL MaNGA spectrum of a particular bursting disk galaxy, allowing us to investigate the link between outflows and star formation. Using an outflow diagnostic, we discovered that the outflow in this galaxy is confined and outflow velocity and mass outflow rates correlate with star formation rate but not with stellar mass. Observations of ionized gas show outflowing regions, circular in shape, located near areas of intense star formation. Deep learning models' efficiency can be enhanced by pre-training them on unrestricted, non-labeled datasets. To date, most research on image analysis has concentrated on image classification due to its simplicity in assessing image content. Conversely, image depth assessment demands that the model incorporates more complex scene structures and spatial hierarchies. We hypothesize that utilizing depth assessment for pre-training might yield benefits not seen with image classification. We support this notion by showing that employing Kornowski et al.'s 2021 method for monocular depth assessment introduces a notable improvement in semantic segmentation performance on standard datasets, specifically PASCAL VOC and PASCAL-Context. Furthermore, we demonstrate that utilizing monocular depth for pre-training is particularly advantageous when employing hierarchical segmentation models, revealing that such techniques capitalize on the rich scene structure information extracted by the depth model. Ultimately, we make mycodes and model weights available so that other researchers can replicate and expand upon these outcomes. They demonstrate that combining a monocular depth model with a low-level scene structure interpreter results in superior performance over traditional pre-training techniques. Consequently, researchers working on semantic segmentation may find it worthwhile to investigate the utilization of monocular depth for pre-training. Moreover, results from a quantitative analysis using Fast and Neural Accessibility Evaluators reveal that high-performance models achieved with monocular depth for pre-training exhibit more accurate assessments of scene complexity, as reflected in the confirmed ranking of model capabilities. In modern vehicular networks, edge intelligence plays a pivotal role. It leverages local processing at edge nodes near the data source to facilitate real-time applications such as traffic management, accident detection, and road condition monitoring. Nevertheless, this intelligent paradigm faces significant hurdles due to privacy concerns stemming from unmasked user identities and intricate topological connections. To overcome these obstacles, this study proposes a comprehensive framework that incorporates private wireless networks and blockchain technology to create a decentralized, blockchain-based Blockchain-based Privacy Preserving Edge Intelligence (BPEI) framework. BPEI provides robust and efficient security, specifically through the creation of a unique identifier for each vehicle. This identifier, known as a Vehicle Public Key, self-evolves over time to maintain user privacy while enabling secure and efficient networking. Furthermore, BPEI enables scalable and efficient data intelligence while maintaining real-time capabilities. To verify the effectiveness of BPEI, an innovative blockchain framework, titled e2-Aggregated Blockchain (e2-AB), is developed. e2-AB boasts impressive performance characteristics, including minimal latency, significant network capacity savings, and substantial processing savings at 5G basebands. By maintaining a 99.99% network reliability level, e2-AB also supports a high throughput of 86% and efficient processing at 99% of existing 5G networks. By incorporating e2-AB in BPEI, users can enjoy substantial cost savings of up to 31%. Finally, numerical computations confirm that BPEI offers considerable latency reductions of up to 3.6 times over conventional intelligence methods. BPEI also preserves user privacy by maintaining an anonymous identity in the vehicular network, achieving private computing at the edge with minimal exposed data to the network. Consequently, BPEI enables users to maintain their privacy while maintaining the integrity and efficiency of the vehicular network. In summary, BPEI offers a robust, efficient, scalable, and private computing framework for contemporary edge intelligence applications in vehicular networks. Its decentralized and blockchain-based approach ensures seamless user anonymity while maintaining real-time intelligence with minimal exposure to the network. Additionally, BPEI provides efficient computing at the edge with user privacy. Consequently, BPEI creates a balance between the benefits of edge intelligence and the risks associated with user privacy. However, BPEI may have some drawbacks, including potential delays in communicating to the blockchain. However, BPEI achieves this through a decentralized approach, which also provides other benefits. Ultimately, BPEI effectively maintains an efficient edge computing paradigm with user privacy

By examining over 200 variations of domain adaptation methods combined with more than 100 pre-trained backbones in three image classification datasets, we evaluate their performance across nine different domain to dataset mappings. Our study reveals that introducing a small adjustment to the backbone's output is generally beneficial and that using multiple instance normalization per layer enhances the accuracy of adapted models. Additionally, we found that adapting models using the cross entropy loss with softmax tends to yield more accurate results. However, the relationships between loss functions and layer-wise normalization methods are still in need of further exploration. For comprehensive replication, our code and dataset are made available at https://github.com/isaacabuffate/dnd-metrics. The peculiar cluster, RXCJ0232.2-4420, situated at a redshift of z=0.28, contains a peculiar mixture of radio sources and unusual substructure. Within this cluster, two large radio sources lie within a line, surrounded by diffuse radio plasma. This unusual configuration raises questions about the source of the radio emission, with possible origins in active galactic nuclei within the central galaxies or shock heating from merging action. We examined the distribution of X-ray count rates in small regions within the cluster to explore its substructure. We conducted two analyses using different areas and radii, but they shared a common goal: to investigate the cluster's substructure by comparing X-ray emissions through two statistical tests. We aimed to determine if the X-ray emissions originate from the same source using these methods. We further compared the distribution of isophotal ellipticities to better understand the shape of the X-ray emissions. By conducting these analyses on four different regions, we aimed to identify the cluster's substructure and characteristics, such as its substructure significance and thermal pressure. We found that three regions showed similar substructure significance and thermal pressure levels, suggesting that the X-ray emissions originate from gas within the cluster. However, the fourth region showed significantly different results, indicating more intense substructure. This region showed a 65% probability of merging or disruption at z=0.28, based on the merger rate for relaxed clusters. By comparing statistical measures, we identified similar patterns in the distribution of radio sources and X-ray emissions. However, the X-ray analyses showed greater variability due to the sample size or statistical methods. Ultimately, the origins of the radio sources remain unclear, but the cluster's characteristics provide valuable insights into its structure. Given the cluster's location on the sky and results from the X-ray analyses, we propose that the radio sources may be the result of active galactic nuclei within galaxies that have merged with the central galaxies. However, further data from spectroscopic surveys would be required to confirm this theory. This study contributes to a greater understanding of the morphology and thermal properties of the cluster by examining different regions and employing various statistical methods to analyze X-ray emissions. Such studies can lead to a more accurate assessment of the cluster's substructure and thermal properties. By conducting these analyses, we can broaden our understanding of galaxy clusters and their characteristics. This research further highlights the significance of relaxing the circular annulus constraint in analyzing X-ray emissions, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the cluster's morphology and thermal properties. The recently proposed Legendre Memory Module exhibits exceptional capacity for
handling complex long-term dependencies and demonstrates solid accuracy on
challenging tasks such as the SHARe benchmark. However, its training process
is characterized by a pronounced non-linear regression characteristic in the
course of its initial phase. This nonlinear regression makes it difficult to
accurately determine the rate at which performance improves. Consequently, it
is difficult to compare the outcomes with substantial theoretical basis. This
difficulty is compounded by the fact that there is a shortage of consensus
regarding the LM's training protocols. To address these challenges, this study
investigates the application of parallel training to the LM. By leveraging
inter-correlations between elements in the initial attended trajectory, this
paper develops a novel method for partitioning the attended trajectory. This
partitioning enables parallel training, thereby eliminating the non-linear
regression observed in the traditional approach. Furthermore, the paper's results
confirm the effectiveness of parallel training at accelerating LM training. Additionally, by employing parallel training, the accuracy of LM models is
shown to be comparable to state-of-the-art models with 20% reduced parameters. This
research facilitates a deeper understanding of the LM's internal workings, and
ultimately, provides a substantial step towards developing standardized testing
for recurrent models and their performance evaluation. Finally, the paper's
outcomes lay the groundwork for enhancing the model's scalability through
distributed training. Experimental validation of the latter, however, remains
outside the scope of this study's current iteration. The proposed method's code
will be made publicly available on GitHub, and further discussion can also be
hosted on this platform for further development.  This study culminates from a

Numerical methods used to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) have inherent limitations in approximating certain complex phenomena. Neural networks, when employed as an alternative, also exhibit similar restrictions despite their potential for more expressive representations. The root of their limited performance lies in the'spectral bias,' a built-in tendency for neural networks to learn low-frequency information first. We have discovered that utilizing a momentum-based optimization approach can mitigate this spectral bias, thus enabling neural networks to more effectively tackle PDE-related tasks. By experimenting with the stationary diffusion equation and focusing on the influence of spectral bias, we were able to develop a theoretical understanding of the problem and identify momentum-driven reductions in reconstruction errors. Additionally, we found that our proposed framework could successfully predict non-linear flows where state-of-the-art methods had failed. Ultimately, this investigation underscores the significance of accounting for the inherent characteristics of the data-generating process in order to unlock the full potential of neural networks. Traditional approaches to robot learning have shown significant benefits but still fall short in providing frameworks for application in industry settings. Specifically, implementing robot skills learned through reinforcement learning remains a major challenge. In our research, we focus on formulating reinforcement learning problems in a way that is easy to understand and easily transferable to other fields. Our proposed method combines model-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning with the ability to identify patterns in data. By integrating induction logic and the creation of generalised decision trees, we aim to develop a groundbreaking framework for a variety of robot tasks. Our work demonstrates promising results on a simulated scenario and showcases its practical applications on a real robotic arm. Our findings highlight the importance of skill hierarchy and the efficiency of our integrated framework in producing understandable policies quickly. Additionally, our research demonstrates the value of using pattern recognition to speed up the process of translating policy knowledge to other domains. Specifically, we have achieved a significant reduction of up to 47 times. In summary, our research provides a novel framework for robot learning and successfully addresses the main difficulties associated with transferring learned skills to other fields. Our method demonstrates that with the correct representation of problems and the use of pattern analysis, it is possible to establish a link between reinforcement learning and other fields such as robotics. Importantly, our research makes it possible to formulate understandable, reusable, and cost-effective knowledge of robot skills. Our work has significant implications for the development of robot skills learned through reinforcement learning. More details about our research can be found at https://dx.com/research/exlm. A novel, non-invasive diagnostic method for identifying brain disorders has been developed through the analysis of magnetic resonance images. The proposed algorithm utilizes a specific template to map the hippocampal regions in MR images and assess their health based on any abnormalities present. To achieve this task, a Multi-Convolutional Neural Network (Multi-CNN) model is designed by combining three Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) in a parallel configuration. The effectiveness of Multi-CNN was evaluated using in-house MR image datasets collected from 106 patients suffering from temporal lobe epilepsy and 106 patients affected by Alzheimer's disease, with ground truth annotations provided by three experts. The findings demonstrate that Multi-CNN accurately identifies hippocampal sub-regions, with a high level of agreement observed between the model and expert annotations. The proposed method performed comparably to other partitioning methods in terms of accuracy, with a mean J-Similarities index of 0.8482 that revealed an 83.02% agreement among the experts. The model's proposed hip-partitioning multi-CNN paradigm has the potential to be applied in other fields, such as Alzheimer's and epilepsy detection. Furthermore, the model can be utilized for overall hippocampal assessment on MR images, enabling the detection of semantic features in Alzheimer's and seizure-generating regions in the seizure zone. Our research focuses on calculating the number of SRAs produced in galactic cosmic rays, their transport to Earth's magnetosphere, and interactions within it. Using GEANT4, we simulate SRA production and capture at low Earth orbit heights, with a particular emphasis on implications for radiation therapy. Our 3D GEANT4 model has been modified to represent the Earth's magnetic field and a simplified solar wind for specific conditions in 2020. By applying this, we've been able to estimate the number of SRAs captured at 400 km altitude, with a finding of approximately 3.77 x 10^9 SRA/hour in the therapeutic radiation range. Moreover, seasonal variations in solar wind result in a 20-fold fluctuation and a strong magnetic field can significantly reduce particle counts, a situation that could offer protection from space radiation. Our research offers the first comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation of SRAs in low Earth orbit capture and provides a valuable tool for modeling the complex interplay of Earth's magnetic field, solar wind, and cosmic radiation. As such, it has the potential to contribute to a broader understanding of space radiation and propose a potential solution for low Earth orbit applications. Recent advancements in graph deep learning show that graph neural networks (GNNs) have excellent performance in handling 3D point cloud data and molecular graphs. To meet the requirements of these problems, we developed a novel deep learning framework that incorporates progressive reduction in spatial resolution and topological structure. This framework combines the global reduction in spatial resolution with the local reconfiguration of topological structure. Consequently, it effectively improves the model's expressiveness and enhances training efficiency. However, the performance of this framework depends on multiple factors, including the choice of sensors for data collection, the complexity of input data, and the reconfiguration of topological structure. Therefore, we designed multiple improved modules to boost the model's performance. Notably, we introduced a new loss function, $\mathcal{L}_{PC}$, and we demonstrated the effectiveness of combining the global reduction in spatial resolution and the reconfiguration of topological structure in enhancing model performance. Experimental results show the superiority of our framework over state-of-the-art methods in 3D point cloud recognition and molecular graph prediction tasks. The well-known Lights Out puzzle is a $nxn$ grid where each cell can be turned on or off by clicking an adjacent cell. We've explored the strategic aspect of this game by introducing two variants of the Maximum Clicks Dilemma. In this research, we revise the principles of Abstract Interpretation by splitting the effects of abstract operators into two distinct phases. We propose an operator that creates an abstract domain and a procedure that applies operations within that domain. This new framework enlarges the class of abstract domains available in existing Abstract Interpretation, as domain homomorphisms can be used with any abstract operator. Furthermore, we develop a general method for generating new abstract domains through a process called extension-addition. We apply our innovative approach to develop domains for approximating reach sets of linear systems with shifts. The resulting analysis surpasses the existing state-of-the-art in set-based analysis of linear systems with shifts. We also provide code for our new abstract domains to facilitate easy evaluation and comparison with existing methods. After conducting thorough examinations, our improved domains were found to outperform or match the best existing domains in six out of seven tests across various system types and scales. However, it's essential to note that our new domains may not offer precise solutions to all analyses, but rather acceptable approximations that are easy to verify. Therefore, if precise accuracy is required, traditional Abstract Interpretation should still be utilized. Ultimately, our technique expands the capabilities of Abstract Interpretation and allows for expanded uses in the field. Research has demonstrated the potential of data augmentation in NLP through controlled language manipulation. This work focuses on developing data augmentation for code-switched texts through altering language mixing patterns. We apply this approach to enhance models dealing with code-switching between Arabic and English. Our study encompasses two main aspects: initially, we have established a dataset containing various forms of code-switched text, which has been collected through altering the original NLC dataset. We have also created multiple sets of control specifications allowing for the definition of code-switching patterns within a sentence. Secondly, we have utilized the HAKE framework to incorporate context-driven principles in word substitution. Specifically, we have investigated different contextual influences - word, sentence, and sentence-to-word context - as factors affecting word replacement during the data generation process. Our experiments have demonstrated that employing contextual word substitution in a word-by-word manner yields more natural outcomes than replacement based solely on words. Moreover, the generated pseudo-data has been found to boost the performance of fully contextualized models, with improved results observed when contextual word-level influences are taken into account. Our findings also suggest that precise code-switching control is key to natural data generation. To facilitate future research, our code and generated data are being made available on our GitHub page. We intend to extend this research by exploring other forms of data augmentation for code-switched texts. Specifically, we aim to combine the effects of flipping syntactic structures and flipping code-switching patterns within sentences to further enhance the quality of generated data. Hex meshes contain two types of elements, hexahedrons and pyramids, which have been extensively researched due to their natural separation into cells and faces. Unlike quadrangle meshes with only one type of element, hex meshes possess distinct facial indices (face tags) that are utilized to distinguish between various types of elements. However, a long-standing issue with hex mesh research stems from the need to separate hex and tetrahedral elements using a cut-off value, which is often applied to elements based on their specific conditions. As a result, a set of elements with indices falling within the defined range can be identified as hexahedrons, while the others are classified as tetrahedra. Unfortunately, this strategy is prone to errors, particularly when hexahedra have narrow ranges and long tails or when tetrahedra exhibit extended and narrow shapes. To overcome these limitations, we present a new method for accurately separating hex and tetrahedral elements by employing a statistical approach that analyzes the distribution of facial indices to distinguish between hex and tetrahedral elements. We tested our proposed method on diverse hex meshes tesselated with up to 58 million hexahedra and 119 million pyramidal elements. The results demonstrate that our approach efficiently identifies pure hexahedral and tetrahedral sub-meshes with minimal computational expense. Furthermore, we have successfully applied this technique to accurately split hybridized mixed-dimensional assemblies into 3D and 1D sub-assemblies. The proposed implementation is currently available on GitHub at https://github.com/mjoecht/hybrid-mesh-decomposition. To the best of our knowledge, this resource provides the largest publicly accessible hybrid-mesh decomposition software to date. We have also utilized the identified tetrahedra to generate surface meshes with a maximum of 89 million facets. The presented decomposition algorithm can be adapted to recognize p-type hybridized mixed-dimensional assemblies consisting of p0 tetrahedra and p0 pyramidal elements and their associated p-1 surface meshes. The idea is to leverage prior knowledge within deep models to infuse learning with continuity. The Coarse-Grained Continuity framework consists of three novel components. Firstly, it defines a quantitative measure of continuity based on Lipschitz continuity in metric spaces. Secondly, it adapts this continuity metric for use in association metrics such as the Pearson correlation and the Fraction of Perfect Solutions (FPS) in the context of reinforcement learning. Thirdly, it develops an innovative method to integrate continuity into the reinforcement learning pipeline. The experimental results in the games of ChessMate-64 and 16x16 Grid Game demonstrate that Coarse-Grained Continuity leads to enhanced sample efficiency when compared to industry-standard randomized smoothing techniques. The source code is available at https://github.com/leharark/Coarse-Grained_Continuity. The research ultimately sheds light on solutions for addressing the challenge of increasing sample efficiency in deep reinforcement learning. Our understanding of the world is shaped by the presence of living beings, which are driven by desires, intentions, emotions, and behaviors guided by innate and learned characteristics. To grasp their essence, we focus on their core as living entities, which is characterized by properties such as vitality, responsiveness, animacy, intentions, and emotions. This paper explores how human visual systems represent and classify inanimate and animate entities, specifically in aspects related to essence-building characteristics. To elucidate, we employed a visual generation framework to create images of concept-fire-essence variations, which were either animate or inanimate, and asked people to identify their animacy without prior explanation. The results revealed that people could accurately recognize inanimate objects and differentiate between various animate classes including humans, animals, and plants, even when the images featured distinct body parts or were masked. Furthermore, map tests revealed that regions crucial for understanding animacy, which are located in the ventral temporal cortex and include the anterior inferior temporal junction, played a critical role in this task. This research indicates that these areas not only recognize individual objects like animals but also recognize categories, which are larger in scope and more complex, which was a surprising discovery. Our findings demonstrate that human visual systems represent inanimate and animate entities as part of a unified structure that encompasses various levels of classification and categories, which are essential for understanding the essence of objects that are central to our interactions with the world. These findings were confirmed through a new task designed to investigate how people mentally organize animacy categories and communicate with each other about them. The results showed that people were able to accurately recognize inanimate and animate entities and also categorize animates into meaningful groups, which are mentally accessible. Moreover, when people were asked to describe their thoughts, their responses revealed that they linked animacy categories to their core characteristics such as the presence of limbs, eyes, or plants. These findings suggest that groups of related concepts, which are organized based on shared properties, have a special role in communicating understanding to others. To explain these findings, we hypothesize that animacy categories are represented as nodes in a large network, which connect concepts based on their essence-building characteristics. This representation aligns with empirical results and offers a theoretical framework for understanding how human visual systems create and classify inanimate and animate entities as part of a unified visual language that is shared among people. This representation can also explain how these concepts are developed from sensory experiences and influenced by cultural factors. To address issues arising from extreme events like shocks and discontinuities in multidimensional simulations, the Arrangement-Preserving Filter is designed. Its primary objective is to maintain the exact solution in smooth areas while modifying the discrete arrangement of singular points. However, the current APF algorithm has a limitation: it can only effectively manage the discrete arrangement in one-dimensional simulations. When attempting multidimensional simulations, it falls short due to complications in identifying the global arrangement of singular points. A novel approach presented in this thesis involves formulating the Arrangement-Preservation Filter as a convex optimization problem. This new strategy requires arranging in a manner that minimizes a specified cost function. Consequently, the discrete arrangement of singular points is determined. Moreover, this method's ability to perform well in multidimensional simulations is corroborated by both theoretical and practical experiments. It is especially proven that under specific conditions, the arrangement obtained through this strategy corresponds to the one-dimensional APF arrangement. To validate its utility, the reformulated APF arrangement is applied to a range of multidimensional test problems. Moreover, its capabilities are also demonstrated in an adaptive finite element solver for hyperbolic conservation laws. Details on both the theoretical and practical assessments can be found in the author's PhD dissertation. Our Insight-HXMT analysis revealed that these fluctuations experienced a significant spectral change, with a peak count rate increase of over 1000 times during the most intense phase. This increase led to a spectral index shift from 2.2 to 3.6 when comparing the hard and soft flux components. Our studies indicate that these fluctuations triggered coronal evolutions through persistent, dynamic instabilities. During these fluctuations, the outer corona's density is expected to have changed by more than two orders of magnitude. This dynamic corona development, in turn, influenced the inner corona's density, with a potential inner-trapping radius shifting by thousands of kilometers. Furthermore, we observed that MAXI J1535-571's outer accretion disk radius underwent a noticeable shift, with a maximum change of over two orders of magnitude in the outer disk radius throughout its entire soft gamma-ray phase. Our Insight-HXMT observations suggest that these fluctuations triggered corona developments via a coronal evaporation mechanism, with evidence of a disk break. With an Insight-HXMT dataset, we confirmed that MAXI J1535-571's fluctuations caused corona developments and further highlighted their significant impact on a outer disk extension via a disk photosphere model. This extension was accompanied by a substantial outer disk radius shift. Our Insight-HXMT analysis provides the first detailed evidence for type-C correlations during coronal evolution, suggesting that these fluctuations play a significant role in maximizing a source's hard X-ray emission. With MAXI J1535-571's observations, we observed that these fluctuations experienced the most significant coronal evolutions, likely due to their dynamic corona development. Nonetheless, we observed notable differences in coronal features between type-B and type-C, suggesting the former may also play a significant role in soft gamma-ray emission. In multi-agent learning systems, ensuring fairness and robustness is crucial for interacting agents, as they often encounter unpredictable behaviors. Training these agents through reinforcement learning alone requires significant data and can lead to biased decision-making. To improve the stability of interacting agents, the concept of intrinsic motivation is introduced, focusing on the sample-wise empowerment achieved when agents exhibit their capabilities. By incorporating this intrinsic motivation into the reinforcement learning framework, the agent's policy becomes more resilient to varying environments and counterparts' behaviors. Our method, known as transfer empowerment, establishes a multi-agent framework that leverages a leader-follower structure. A robust follower uses the empowerment as intrinsic motivation in its reinforcement learning, while being treated as a black-box system. Meanwhile, the leader also learns through a similar approach but considers the variable parameters of its partner as additional aspects of the environment. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in withstanding fluctuations in environments and counterpart behaviors, as evidenced by its application in learning to cooperate in the task. Additionally, the proposed method's properties are theoretically analyzed, providing insights into its performance. Our approach is evaluated using a multi-task learning scenario with the cooperative task of shared controller driving, utilizing a physical racing game as the testing ground, and our code can be found at https://github.com/idealsail/TEL-Dynamic.pdf. By dependably adapting to changing environments and behaviors of its partner, the re-responding agent achieves superior sample efficiency, as shown by our empirical results. Furthermore, due to its sample efficiency, the learning process can be optimized via analysis within a multi-task framework. Our approach exhibits properties that are beneficial for common policy learning methods in the presence of random behaviors. Our contribution to the multi-agent learning community is the introduction of an innovative intrinsic motivation mechanism addressing the issue of handling unpredictable behaviors. Additionally, the properties of our approach are theoretically justified through multiple generalization results that could benefit other algorithms in the future. One potential area for improvement would be the integration of our method into the dynamics of reinforcement learning to enhance the fairness and robustness of interacting agents. Our knowledge gained from analyzing our method could also be applied to develop a framework for benchmarking the fairness and robustness of multi-agent learning algorithms. A potential extension of our approach would be the generalization of the concept of intrinsic motivation in the context of distributed reinforcement learning. Our results could also be used to improve the design of AI agents working in domains with unpredictable environments and behaviors. Our knowledge could also be applied to develop a framework for evaluating the fairness and robustness of learning algorithms.

In various fields such as chemistry, materials science, and cosmetics, identifying unknown substances from spectral datasets is a significant challenge. Existing techniques like deep learning-based methods rely on having a sizeable dataset for each category. However, this poses an issue when dealing with a wide range of complex data, as gathering sufficient data for every possible scenario is impractical. Our study focuses on identifying spectral data of substances that have not been previously seen before, without requiring extensive data collection. To address this, we introduce a new approach utilizing contrastive learning based on physical simulations. Our model, SubSpec-OA, simulates spectral data for all possible substances and learns to recognize real samples by identifying similar scenarios. SubSpec-OA was successfully tested on various datasets and conditions, achieving one-shot generalization and showcasing its superiority over other methods. Additionally, we created a publicly accessible web platform that allows users to input spectral data and accurately identify the substance's composition. This breakthrough can benefit a variety of fields by providing accurate identification of substances using spectral data, regardless of the expertise or knowledge level. The study's code and platform can be accessed at https://github.com/ByuiJo/SubSpec-OA. The platform is live at https://subspec-oa.byujoo.com.

We introduce a novel, detector-free method for object matching, which directly uses image embeddings from any feature extractor to calculate correspondence between objects in two images. Our approach, LoFTR, stands out for its simplicity and efficiency, requiring no tuning of hyperparameters. It also works effectively across a wide range of objects and scenes. Calibration is not needed and the method is robust to objects with significant changes in appearance. This is enabled by our use of a specific matching function based on the Local Aggregate Transformer. We show that our method outperforms existing approaches in various object matching datasets in multiple categories. Our method can run at very high frame rates on consumer-grade computers. For more information, refer to our project page at https://pfafsi-cmu.github.io/LoFTR/. LoFTR is also available as an open-source library at https://github.com/PFAhsi-CMU/LoFTR.

To improve the efficiency of distributed generation management and reduce energy losses, it is crucial to optimize residential energy consumption. This can be effectively achieved through independent demand side management. In this research, a more realistic and precise model is developed to simulate energy usage and various constraints of residential areas. Based on this model, a collective game framework is established to determine optimal load schedules that minimize overall energy usage and a new metric, known as real-time load charging, is introduced to incentivize participants. The study shows that the proposed approach not only reduces energy consumption and variance but also decreases peak demand and provides quantitative results for validation. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the developed strategy allows participants to benefit economically from their energy management. Lastly, the impact of various key parameters on system efficiency is analyzed through numerical simulations. A demonstration example and the corresponding MATLAB code are provided to illustrate the method's implementation. The outcome of this research reveals that by utilizing game theory and load charging, residential energy consumption can be optimized and reduced. This approach not only lowers energy usage and peak demand but also decreases energy loss and environmental pollution. It has the ability to economically benefit participants and it is an independent, decentralized method that can be widely applied. It is suitable for areas with or without distribution companies and it is an efficient way to optimize residential energy consumption. This study contributes to the development of a cost-effective strategy for optimizing residential energy consumption. It proposes an efficient approach to minimize energy usage and a new real-time load charging method to incentivize participants. The impact of various key parameters on system efficiency and users' energy benefits and consumption variance are analyzed. It is proven that under specific conditions, the optimal energy usage schedule can be achieved. The authors believe that the complexity of residential areas can be effectively optimized through energy scheduling. It is hoped in the future to develop more intuitive methods for determining the second derivative of the energy cost function. This study and its outcomes may contribute to the optimization of residential energy systems. It is recommended for further research on distributed generation and future smart grids equipped with advanced management systems and decentralized optimization algorithms. It is also suggested for the integration of more complex constraints of residential areas and land charging models in future work. The proposed approach can be considered as a practical solution in the development of smart grids and it is also an efficient way to minimize residential energy consumption. It is suitable for areas with or without distribution companies and it is an independent, decentralized method that can be widely applied. It is also worth exploring Energy Storage in residential homes to provide a positive contribution to the development of smart grids.

We investigated the influence of gravity in the Gullstrand-Penrose metric on the Hawking surface and particle emission from charged black strings within the framework of Rastall theory of gravity. We found that for sufficiently high charges, the black string can exhibit de Sitter behavior at the core, resolving the apparent singularity. Considering the impact of revised gravitational forces on the thermodynamics of these black strings, we evaluated the Hawking radiation boundary by finding the proper affine parameter, thus establishing the Larmor factor for the emission spectrum. Consequently, we analyzed the effect of gravitational redshift on the spectrum. Wildfires pose significant threats to nature and infrastructure worldwide. 
To quantify global wildfire risk, we evaluated the magnitude of active wildfire areas from 2003 to 2021, focusing on spatial and temporal intensity patterns. 
A novel, straightforward metric called the Fire Index was proposed to measure seasonal intensity as the average daily number of fires within a 5x5 km area. 
This index allows for cross-regional comparisons that are not influenced by local factors. 
Geostatistical modeling revealed that global wildfire intensity follows a temperature-driven sinusoidal pattern, influenced by solar radiation and geographical location. 
The accuracy of our fire prediction model was validated through retrospective testing, achieving an r-value of 0.87 for the training data and 0.16 for the test data. 
This research lays foundation for the creation of an internationally recognized early warning system for wildfires. 
The study findings and methodology are now openly available to support decision-making at the national and international levels. 
Future developments will focus on expanding the study to include additional countries and data sources to further improve the accuracy of wildfire prediction. 
A limitation of our study is the reliance on a single, publicly accessible database, restricting the scope of potential improvements. 
Therefore, incorporating supplementary data sources holds considerable potential to further refine the fire intensity predictions." - Authors.

A significant challenge in reinforcement learning is reward learning. This task becomes even more difficult when reward labels are scarce and complex in real-world applications. This study introduces VACRank, a technique that clusters similar trajectories based on visual representations to efficiently rank actions and speed up reward learning. The process involves two steps: first, it establishes a connection between state and penetration values to create visually-driven sub-trajectories; then, it leverages neural networks to predict optimal sub-trajectories. The system utilizes a penalty loss to optimize the ranking of clustered trajectories, using a penalty-based loss function in conjunction with state features to train this ranking task. Experimental results show that VACRank achieves better performance than comparable approaches, with significant time savings in ranking. The approach also surpasses a baseline method in learning a continuous reward function for autonomous driving. The study includes comprehensive evaluations to provide an in-depth understanding of VACRank's performance. The approach outperforms other techniques in trajectory clustering tasks, with extensive empirical analysis available on the authors' website. The method has been successfully applied in an industry setting to automate the ranking of action sequences for the domain of autonomous driving. This work has been published at the IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Vehicles 2021. The corresponding paper can be found at arXiv:2103.16164. The approach described here received the 1st place award in TrajectoryRanking at the Autonomous Driving Challenge at ICIV 2021. The method is now in active use at Baidu Autonomous Driving as a key component of their automated feature generation process. The corresponding code can be found at https://aicook.github.io/. We investigate the statistical properties of the eigenspectra of family of non-Hermitian matrices featuring small-rank perturbations of quasi-Hermitian band matrices. These matrix families can be considered intermediate between Hermitian and non-Hermitian matrix perturbations in terms of rank. This intermediate case offers unique characteristics, particularly concerning isospectral metric behavior, distinct from purely Hermitian or non-Hermitian perturbations. Building upon the sigma-model approximation established in [7], we examine isospectral metrics, eigenvalue spacing, and spectral rigidity across various system parameters, including band width, matrix size, and perturbation magnitude. Notably, we explore the sigma-model's convergence in this setting and its impact on the discussed statistical properties. This investigation is facilitated by the significant conceptual and technical advancements presented in [21, 22], which serve as the foundation for our work. Moreover, to validate the sigma-model approximation, we calculate the leading-order correction to eigenspectrum integrals in terms of the epsilon parameter, which governs the sigma-model's gradient expansion. This correction is analogous to the bulk-edge anomaly correction found in topological system theories. Approximately, this correction is expressed as Wigner surfer's six-fold integral, with the topological correction being proportional to the topological invariant, with the proportionality constant determined from eigenvalue polynomial expansions. This topological correction dominates the leading-order term for all tested cases. After confirming the sigma-model's convergence, we utilize it to assess the asymptotic behavior of the discussed statistical properties, specifically expressing eigenspectra, eigenvalue spacing, and spectral rigidity in terms of the epsilon parameter. Notably, our analysis reveals that some properties exhibit logarithmic asymptotic behavior with the epsilon parameter. Consequently, this behavior may be attributed to an artifact of sigma-model approximation. Consequently, we anticipate that this aspect of our results may be modified once the limited-dimensionality aspect of our problem is accounted for. Notably, we also discover that within the sigma-model framework, isospectral metric, eigenvalue spacing, and spectral rigidity exhibit topological corrections that may alter our previous conclusions concerning these properties' asymptotic behaviors. Our analysis will be based on numerical simulations, which provide conclusive evidence of the discussed corrections. To improve conversation comprehension, many pre-trained models have been developed. Despite their effectiveness, current models struggle to generalize due to their reliance on limited conversational data. We argue that strong conversation understanding requires a solid foundation in language understanding and semantic analysis. In this study, we introduce an enhanced conversation comprehension pre-training approach that incorporates datasets from eight distinct semantic tasks, notably using the PrAGMATIC and RoBERTa datasets. Our innovative method successfully demonstrates superior performance across various benchmarks and real-world applications, notably a significant 6.7 points improvement in the SocialIQA metric. Furthermore, to facilitate future replication, we publicly release our model, experiment logs, and sample code. The model will be made available through the Zenodo repository. 

The key contributions of this study are threefold:
Pre-training with the PrAGMATIC dataset significantly enhances conversation comprehension.
A novel pre-training approach combining the RoBERTA and PrAGMATIC models leads to remarkable results in processing conversational data and also enhances general language comprehension.
The proposed model demonstrates exceptional performance across various benchmarks and real-world applications, underscoring its reliability and versatility. 

In addition to these contributions, we note that current conversation comprehension models often evaluate too narrowly, focusing primarily on task-oriented discussions. In contrast, many real-world conversations revolve around shared interests and involve topic-based exchanges. As such, we introduce a comprehensive evaluation framework consisting of eight diverse datasets to assess a model's ability to process conversations effectively. Moreover, we manually categorize the underlying themes of the SocialIQA dataset to illustrate the significance of semantic foundations in conversation comprehension. Ultimately, we advocate for a more expansive evaluation in the field of conversation comprehension. The proposed evaluation framework will be made available through the Zenodo repository.

While classical physics assumes a well-defined, complete state, quantum physics represents such uncertainty as a probability distribution.  This letter discusses inferences regarding unknowns in quantum physics, particularly in scenarios where initial information is limited.  Two popular methods for drawing conclusions about unknowns in quantum physics are the Bayes' theorem approach and the Dirac-like approach.  Neither of these methods was originally derived within a probabilistic framework.  We address whether these methods for drawing conclusions are consistent with one another, referring to such consistency as 'post-inferential consistency'.  This concept is seen as a special instance of 'inference consistency', a broader idea studied in the field of probabilistic reasoning.  To explore post-inferential consistency, we consider three questions.  Firstly, do the Bayes' theorem and Dirac-like methods for drawing conclusions agree? In cloud computing environments, where virtualized resources manage workloads as a service, ensuring fair and efficient allocation of computing resources is crucial. VM reservations allow for guaranteed access to allocated resources, while charge-for-use billing models generate significant revenue for cloud service providers. Since users typically reserve a total amount of resources, dividing it equally among applications can optimize usage and increase user satisfaction. This concept is referred to as prepartition. The current approach assigns resources by prepartitioning them and reserving the remaining amount through slot-partitioning. The effectiveness of prepartitioning is evaluated through comparisons with the slot-partitioning method and scheduling without reservations. The results show that prepartitioning achieves the highest resource utilization and makes the most of the available resources, outperforming slot-partitioning and baseline scheduling. Moreover, experiment data confirm that prepartitioning generates less context switchings compared to slot-partitioning. The impact of different parameters such as traffic patterns, scaling factors, and reservation ratios on the performance of prepartitioning is also investigated. The analysis of these experiments reveals that prepartitioning performance benefits from linearly increasing resource utilization with increasing scaling factors, but is less affected by varying reservation ratios, and that different traffic patterns influence the behavior of prepartitioning. The additional insight from this analysis reveals that prepartitioning performance might be impaired by qsort-based workloads and that due to prepartitioning's guaranteed and equal CPU allocation to applications during scheduling, it tends to perform better on workloads with short and uniform job creation. The phenomenon of "wobbling stars" - where a star's velocity and proper motion indicate it has a hidden companion - presents an intriguing opportunity to expand our understanding of these systems. By analyzing the accelerating motion of single stars, the misalignment of velocity and proper motion can be fully explained. Our study involved a review of 121 candidate systems from the "HOTSTARs" sample, which is comprised of early-type, nearby, and fast-moving stars. Through this examination, we were able to recreate the orbital parameterizations for 63 "HOTSTARs" using archival data, including IR and K2 light curves. By applying statistical calculations, we established a limiting mass of 0.13 solar masses and a maximum distance of 180 parsecs for the hidden companions. Our results also indicate that the vast majority of these systems will have not yet reached their orbital equilibrium due to the "velocity-proper-motion alignment test". Moreover, at a distance of 180 parsecs, we observed that the hidden companions of "HOTSTARs" tend to have longer orbital periods. Our study further explores the possibilities of the "hot Jupiters" formation model and the evolution of the binary systems. Ultimately, the findings of this study underscore the significance of analyzing accelerating motion in "HOTSTARs" - providing valuable insights into the characteristics and orbital periods of hidden companions, which makes them ideal subjects for the study of exoplanetary systems. In this paper, we investigate a combination of these models, referred to as the minimal square variational Bayesian autoencoder, which applies a two-stage procedure to switch between learning and inference tasks. A widely employed modulation technique in massive MIMO systems uses $M$-ary amplitude-shift keying with gray coding map. Although easily implementable, this method has drawn less attention due to limitations in its code mapping. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach called GCE is proposed. In this technique, the binary indices of the modulation symbols are encoded using a unique gray coding map. The proposed approach is further enhanced by a low-bit encoding method that takes advantage of the computational efficiency of binary operations. To minimize encoding overhead, a new approach called LOBE is presented. On the other hand, addressing the receive detection loss and quantization feedback issues in adaptive quantization is the primary aim of another proposed technique, called ACCQ. In ACCQ, analog-to-digital converters provide precise channel state information by converting the analog received signal into multiple-bit L-values. Following this, an autoencoder learns the relationships between the input and output variables to provide feedback to ADCs. A label-altered version of an autoencoder called LAE is proposed for this purpose. Although promising, the accuracy of both Deep Learning-based approaches can be improved. Therefore, an integrated version called SMART is presented. By combining the GCE-LOBE and ACCQ-LAE methods, the performance of the proposed technique is demonstrated to be similar to that of having perfect quantization or feedback. Finally, a comparison of the techniques in terms of implementation and memory requirements shows that GCE-LOBE requires significantly less memory and operations than the other methods. Therefore, it is the preferred choice for the context. Crowdsourced labeling, commonly used for machine learning tasks, can be plagued by inconsistent labels due to lack of expertise or ambiguity in concept understanding. This study presents an approach utilizing entropy-based measures to evaluate reliability of individual examples in crowdsourced datasets. The objective is to apply statistical methods to gauge label accuracy, filter noisy data, and enhance model performance. Our method involves generating probability distributions through crowdsourcing, having crowd members assign confidence values to their labels, and combining these values into a reliable, uncertainty-aware class distribution, referred to as 'human softmax'. This process is utilized to train machine learning models starting from scratch, as well as improve already existing models. An additional entropic filter is applied to remove noisy data, and the approach is evaluated with positive results on datasets including MNIST, MNIST-F, and MNIST-FF. Our 'human softmax' method also enables the development of an adaptable, out-of-domain anomaly detection system for x-ray imaging. The proposed technique is a versatile tool allowing for reliable dataset quality assessment, which in turn facilitates robust model development. Furthermore, our approach has the added benefit of facilitating research into dataset mutli-task capabilities and the exploration of anomaly detection, reconstruction, and afolite detection tasks within already existing datasets. A computer-driven approach, guided genetic optimization, efficiently identifies specific adjustments to widely-used C++ compilers that significantly reduce the frequency and severity of critical program failures on widely-used platforms, including Linux and Windows/x64. This report details our investigation into a genetic optimization tool originally designed to enhance the reliability of programs by minimizing the number of crashes they experience. Our examination involved extensive testing spanning 24 hours, examining its ability to replicate original failure reports and identify relevant system libraries involved. Out of 428 tested modifications, the tool successfully replicated original failure reports with 25% of tested configurations, and additionally pinpointed relevant system libraries in 75% of those cases. Furthermore, we observed that the tool often struggles to replicate failures on already-stable code, but yielded promising preliminary results in our replication effort. Our study underscores the importance of further research in the domain of guided genetic optimization for automated software verification and testing. Code and experimental data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.737301. Unlike the original investigation, our replication was accomplished in a matter of hours rather than days, allowing us to tackle more complex challenges with existing techniques, thereby validating the underlying approach.
