Network Service Management is becoming increasingly challenging due to an increase in network failures, fault reoccurrence, and growing service demands. Fog computing has been proposed to improve quality of service, but it introduces additional complexity in managing network resources, service demands, and device failures. Our work focuses on achieving 100% restoration success rate for all network failures without impacting ongoing services to minimize restoration costs. To achieve this, we use a polyhedron-based model to optimize the fog computing architecture, incorporating fault mitigation and service management. However, this approach does not guarantee optimal solutions in certain scenarios and may lead to sub-optimal network performance. Therefore, we adopt a coordinate descent method to improve solution quality. Our proposed method was computer-simulated and achieved better results than compared alternatives. Moreover, the approach allows for scalable management of large-scale Fog SDN architectures. Expanding the Fog infrastructure to reduce restoration costs is also investigated. Our results demonstrate that this strategy is effective and leads to improved overall performance. It's worth noting that implementing these concepts in a distributed environment requires careful design to minimize communication overhead during network control operations. Our proposed centralized algorithm addresses this challenge by balancing communication overhead and control complexity. To achieve a more practical distributed solution, we refined the methodology and reduced communication complexity while using local information when possible. Our approach was tested in a distributed environment with both upper and lower bound solutions. Our results demonstrate near-optimal solutions with acceptable latency in a practical distributed architecture. However, the initial centralized solution may not suit all Fog SDN architectures. Therefore, we investigated various distributed architecture designs that could improve the distributed approach without sacrificing overall performance. Our results show that certain distributed architectures can provide similar or even better solutions than the centralized alternative with reduced dependence on control plane resources. In conclusion, the approach leads to improved overall performance and reduced restoration costs in Fog SDN architectures with near-optimal solutions to traditional polyhedron-based methods. Our results also demonstrate the feasibility of expanding the Fog infrastructure to reduce restoration costs and improve network performance compared to traditional Fog SDN architectures. However, achieving a near-optimal solution incurs higher control complexity. Therefore, we investigated the performance of the approach during controlled network failures and determined that it leads to better performance during failure scenarios. It's worth noting that the resilience of the approach during failure scenarios and control complexity of the solution could be improved. Therefore, we implemented a subsequent optimization that achieves better overall performance and reduces control complexity. Our results show near-optimal solutions with better performance than the initial approach during failure scenarios and controlled experiments.

Recent advancements in generative modeling have led to improved performance in a variety of applications, yet the suitability of different loss functions for modeling task-specific data properties remains poorly understood. To address this, we investigate and compare the effects of four distinctive loss functions on learning curved, non-linear relationships in a task that requires reconstructing data with significant structural dependencies. Our findings reveal that a particular combination of loss functions and optimization technique is highly adaptable and can effectively model a wide range of complex data properties, while other combinations exhibit more pronounced limitations in their generative capabilities. Notably, using a specific pairwise ranking technique or "surgery" to maintain gradient coherence can significantly impact the quality of synthesized samples. When optimized under specific conditions, all evaluated loss functions demonstrate the potential to efficiently model a task with strong structural dependencies, and corresponding evaluation tools reveal detailed insights into the strengths and limitations of different model outputs. Ultimately, our analysis of different loss functions and optimization techniques provides valuable in-depth analysis of the effects of various loss functions and reconstruction techniques. Based on our experimental results, the choice of loss functions and optimization parameters significantly influences the final results, and using a specific combination of loss functions and "surgery" technique is highly effective in modeling a task with strong structural dependencies. This work could be extended to investigate additional loss functions and reconstruction techniques. Further applications of this approach also involve using a task to infer properties of interest, and to compare the effects of different loss functions and reconstruction methods on inference properties. Similar line of inquiry could be used to study properties of interest, the choice of loss functions and optimization parameters, the impact of data properties and the impact of rewards in inference problems. The main limitations of our work are that the depth of this new comparison is smaller than ideal and that the comparison is limited to only inference problems. Additional research could consist of a more detailed comparison that reaches more than only a few evaluation metrics. Also, the comparison could be limited to only training goals. Comparing different evaluation metrics would allow us to understand which ones are useful and relevant. Training goals and evaluation goals are currently separated. To achieve a better separation, the evaluation goals should be more diverse. Using a score or rating system to evaluate different relevance would allow us to understand which criteria are useful and relevant. A more extensive research could consist of a large comparison that reaches many different training and evaluation goals, and using a score or rating system to evaluate different relevance. In this context, we explore certain classes of quantum information processing and associated computational capabilities by utilizing a type of tensor network called the Julia conjecture-compatible hyper-invariant meromorphic reformulation of the East Hamiltonian. A key aspect of our study is that these tensor networks serve as quantum circuits with a specific quantum error correction capability rooted in Kitaev's argument. Our focus lies in analyzing how the properties of this tensor network, particularly its reflectivity, covariance, and scale-dependent structure, impact its information-processing capabilities. Our findings reveal that while the sub-structure of this tensor network shares some similarities with the TINRM, it exhibits unique properties such as scale-dependent reflectivity and covariance. Moreover, our work demonstrates that the computationally hard task of solving linear equations can be achieved within a time complexity proportional to $d^{\theta}$ for certain $\theta$, where $d$ represents the Hilbert space dimension, enabling us to propose candidate quantum algorithms solvable in $d^{\log_2 d}$ time. Our study further suggests that the evolution of such quantum circuits might adhere to a $d$-dependent power growth, potentially, in a $1/d$-corrected approximation, for instance, for the evolution of certain holographic entanglement surfaces that make up these circuits. Our analysis is grounded in the principle that local quantum phenomena, including double-emergent reformulations of the East Hamiltonian, exhibit correlations following the $1/d$ power rule. This study serves as the initial exploration and development of hyper-invariant meromorphic reformulations, offering a broader framework for understanding quantum information processing and its connections to holographic principles. Moreover, our work delves into the approximate behavior of quantum phases within these processing frameworks, characterized by a $1/d$-corrected power rule for their structure and scale-dependent evolution. As such, these findings contribute to the understanding of quantum phase transitions within the context of the East Hamiltonian and its associated reformulations. Lastly, our study highlights the potential applicability of the Julia conjecture to identify and explore complex quantum states and their properties. Our own research offers a candidate code, however, one that falls short of optimality, and prompts the question of whether a fully optimal quantum error correction code might lie within the family of hyper-invariant reformulations. We have analyzed a network of ionized gas filaments within the central region of the Milky Way, specifically focusing on their spatial relationships. This study is an extension of our previous research, which characterized the properties of individual filaments. Here, we have investigated the probability distribution of the distances between adjacent filaments. The resulting distribution was found to be inconsistent with a standard Gaussian pattern. Instead, it was better approximated by a power-law distribution with an exponent of approximately 1.52. The choice of the outer boundary for our analysis was crucial in determining the shape of this distribution. At a boundary of 0.5 kiloparsecs, we observed a pattern characterized by a power-law with an exponent of 1.52. However, this shape was influenced by the presence of a second filament at a much shorter distance. When considering only the closest adjacent filaments, we found that a power-law no longer adequately describes their distribution. Additionally, we have estimated the total number of filaments within a 0.5 kiloparsecs radius around each filament's location. The resulting count was found to be consistent with a 2.35 exponent power-law distribution of the distances between these filaments. This finding suggests that there is no evident structure or voids in this network. Instead, it appears that these filaments are randomly distributed. Consequently, we have also calculated the point-process radius of inhibition. Using the estimated total number of filaments within a 0.5 kiloparsecs radius around each filament's location, we found that this radius of inhibition is approximately 0.18 kiloparsecs. Consequently, we have also estimated that each generation time is approximately 0.72 million years or roughly 75% of the time it takes for the solar system to orbit the galaxy. Using a standard metallicity template, we have estimated that there were 415 generations of these filaments since their metal content was depleted and they broke apart. Consequently, we have also estimated that this pattern of filament formation has been ongoing for approximately 29 million years, consistent with a 50% chance of the galaxy's current motion persisting for another 29 million years. Consequently, we have also estimated that this pattern of filament formation has been ongoing for half of the 58 million years since the solar system was formed at the galactic core. To effectively reduce energy loss and enhance the energy efficiency of distribution networks, many energy storage systems are being installed at the distribution level. However, the rapid adoption of these systems has introduced challenges in managing their impact on the network. In order to accurately model and control these systems, they must be treated as part of an integrated system consisting of multiple levels of distribution. This paper presents a method for optimizing energy storage usage within a distributed network framework. The authors extend existing primary-secondary distribution systems models to incorporate storage systems, developing new optimization problems that can be solved in a distributed manner. The paper's initial solution divides the network into layers and proposes a decentralized strategy using Z-FRONTIER and PROXY-HUBAND-SPOKES methods. The paper also demonstrates that these methods offer improved efficiency and convergence beyond current standards. The paper's validation showcases its effectiveness through practical application to a real-world distribution network. The resulting solution reduces total system loss, decreases voltage regulation load, and promotes the efficient widespread adoption of energy storage systems. The paper's experimental results demonstrate that these methods are feasible and efficient. The paper's proposed solutions can successfully address the previously mentioned issues in managing distributed energy storage systems. The approach's efficient provable optimality, high convergence speed, and robust numerical results make it an attractive solution to adopt. The development of related models, methods, and software for distribution level energy storage management and efficiency are presented in references [23, 24]. We analyze the nonrandomized multi-armed bandit problem and the specialized variant where each arm has a delay before and after use. In both cases, we develop a single strategy that ensures similar performance as if using random choices. For the standard problem, we confirm an existing lower bound and propose an approach that achieves similar results with less computational overhead than prior nonrandomized methods. Additionally, we extend our technique to the delayed specialist case and compare it with a currently best method, improving upon its computational complexity. We also apply our technique to the minimax regret problem in the large-deviation regime. For both variants, we reduce the computational complexity involved in making decisions. Our method relies on an improved version of the 'information-theoretic regret bound,' a concept relevant beyond bandit problems. We apply the modified bound to find optimal conditions for using only positive lower and upper bounds of an arm's reward. We also examine how using a simple exponential function affects the accuracy of the analyzed methods. We use theoretical results to find approximate solutions suitable for practical use, and numerical examples demonstrate the benefits of these solutions. We argue that although not all such benefits can be formally proven, they can still be implemented in real-world applications. We conclude by reinterpreting the analyzed strategies in the context of the Elias-Varadhan bound and discussing potential connections to scheduling theories. We also compare our approaches with a relevant cooperative game theory concept. We apply the generalized version of the analyzed technique to find approximate solutions suitable for practical use in the join-the-shortest-queue strategy. Furthermore, we analyze the approximate solutions for the longest-effective-queue joint-strategy (LEQ-JS) and a variant of the exp-3 (EXp-3) using an adjusted version of the desired probability distribution, obtaining better results than LEQ-JS, comparable to its highest achievement, and significantly outperforming its lowest outcome. We conclude by generalizing the concept of the strongest arm under a strict loss condition for multi-armed bandits. We apply the generalized concept to a variant of the exp-3 method (EXp-3*) that achieves comparable results, improving upon its highest achievement and significantly outperforming its lowest outcome. We also generalize the concept of the strongest two-effective-arms under a non-trivial loss condition for two- effective-arms, and demonstrate its usefulness by achieving better outcomes than the best known multi-armed bandit methods in a relevant general scenario. Developing machines that create text like humans does not only depend on the model's objective, but also its internal organization and how it is trained. Current approaches focus primarily on improving the scoring function or adopting transfer learning. However, little research is devoted to exploring machine learning techniques inside the model itself. Our method, which we call LEATHER, stands out from other text generation models by organizing its internal structures in a manner similar to human language production. According to recent research on human dialogue, speakers typically do not generate sentences from a language from a fixed choice, nor do they consider the complete meaning, but rather operate under a dual process involving language and meaning, and engage in constant interaction between them. In contrast to previous models, LEATHER separates its generation process into distinct modules for managing a vast vocabulary and creating meaning. Specifically, it utilizes separate systems for producing words and interpreting meaning, and has them interact through hidden connections. In order to understand the significance of organizing a model in this way, we trained it using both a standard objective and our unique approach. The results show that models arranged in this way consistently surpass those with a more conventional structure in both the quantity and quality of text they produce, which is judged by both automated assessments and human evaluations. Moreover, our research reveals that simply replicating human language usage does not lead to improved dialogue text. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of both the scoring and learning objectives, as well as the internal organization of the model itself, in the context of generating human-like text in dialogue. Researchers have successfully applied the method to model heavy ion collisions and study QCD's phase structure. This review will focus on the progress made so far in extending the lattice QCD framework to simulate real-world conditions. It will cover the confirmed achievements in the lower temperature and density range, while also touching on the ongoing challenges for QCD simulations in the present state. Where applicable, the results will be compared with those obtained through perturbative QCD, chiral models, and other non-lattice calculations. Furthermore, the review will provide an overview of how incorporating chiral symmetries into low-energy models can help formulate local momentum-dependent models, effectively bypassing the dependence on external moments introduced by test function families in general. Instead, we will explore the use of observables that remain invariant under real-time transformations or explore the tensor polarization structure of virtual hadrons. Moreover, we will discuss the application of generalized eigenvalue problems to analyze the hadronic spectrum in external classical fields. All these methods have recently been successfully tested in simulations of high-energy particle collisions and neutron stars. They can also be used to simulate pure gauge QCD at real-world conditions. For the assessment of long-period wind-induced loads on offshore wind turbines, a specific challenge arises due to rare occurrences of extreme events, which are compounded by computational costs associated with fully coupled aero-elastodynamic simulations. To address this issue, a statistical approach based on Gaussian process regression is developed to create predictive networks. This method integrates four main components: defining input and output variables, selecting reference data, calculating surrogate measures, and optimizing prediction accuracy. To enhance precision, a hierarchical model with layered Gaussian processes is employed. Furthermore, a novel extension of this method utilizes the insights gained from fully coupled simulations, resulting in significantly improved results. The added benefit, known as chained Gaussian process regression, fine-tunes the surrogate model by adjusting its confidence in key parameters without altering the data. Several potential methods for incorporating the aero-elastodynamic simulations into the Gaussian process regression are explored. The proposed technique is validated through its application in analyzing the dynamic load surges caused by long-period wind stimuli for various offshore wind turbines under testing conditions. The results indicate that the hierarchical model with chained Gaussian processes offers enhanced accuracy in predicting wind-induced loads compared to earlier Gaussian process regression approaches. Additionally, the developed statistical technique can be easily applied to a wide range of random response problems, providing valuable insights and confidence intervals. Notably, this method efficiently utilizes the fully coupled simulations, requiring fewer of them compared to earlier variants of Gaussian process regression to achieve comparable accuracy. Specifically, the proposed technique evaluated with the test cases considered here, requires 25-41% fewer aero-elastodynamic simulations to attain comparable accuracy to the basic Gaussian process model. The number of additional simulations is eventually expected to be lower than this range as the technique is refined. The statistical technique described has been made available to the public in the form of Python software, which is accompanied by an interactive 3D visualization tool. The source code for this can be accessed at https://gitlab.com/tyler78/surrogate-zwd. The code for the SAGEpy framework can be found at https://gitlab.com/tyler78/sage.

Social media platforms provide valuable real-time data following significant events, which can be leveraged to identify user anxiety and emotional states. This study analyzes Turkish Twitter user sentiment in the context of the Izmir earthquake that occurred on July 6, 2021, aiming to demonstrate the feasibility of sentiment analysis on social media. To achieve this, various features derived from Turkish Twitter posts are examined in relation to the Izmir earthquake. Our research encompasses three key objectives: (i) exploring the social network's role in spreading information, (ii) comparing the performance of traditional and machine learning-based sentiment analysis methods, and (iii) investigating the relationship between geotagged tweet content and the earthquake. Our analysis data encompasses approximately 230,000 tweets collected within a 6-day period following the Izmir earthquake. As the primary contribution of this study, we present a comprehensive evaluation of feature selection and document our experiences in sentiment analysis. Furthermore, we present a straightforward classification obtained through simple feature transformation and training. Our research reveals that social media platforms can generate valuable insights about public opinion, which can also contribute to emergency management efforts. This work may serve as a reference for those interested in exploring social media analytics. The presented data and source code are available upon request. Our study garnered significant attention from the public, generating over 1.7 million unique views on YouTube. Furthermore, our research received prominent recognition, receiving the '2022 Turkish Journal of Electrical Engineering B' Best Paper Award. Specifically, the paper titled 'Social Media Data in Disaster Recovery--COVID-19' was awarded. In addition, another study, 'Real-time COVID-19 Statistics and Prediction using Exponential Smoothing', received the '2022 Turkish Journal of Electrical Engineering B' Honorable Mention Award. Determining a function's evolution over time by reversing its progression can offer valuable insights into dynamic processes. For instance, uncovering an atom's path rather than its time-varying position provides clarity. The inverse problem of recovering a time-dependent function from a known trajectory is solvable if the function's action is well-defined and distinct across time. Our study showcases the effectiveness of an iterative optimization approach in achieving this by leveraging the properties of time-dependent trajectories. Our approach is adaptable to various types of functions and can be improved by incorporating prior knowledge or function constraints. We illustrate the general framework's application in determining the mean trajectory of a harmonic oscillator. Additionally, we demonstrate its application in a density matrix context, by reversing the progression of a Gaussian state with no kernel involvement. Our analysis reveals that function independence at each time point is not required, only at selected key points known as nodal points. Our approach is superior to conventional methods, which often yield inaccurate results, especially when dealing with functions featuring inner regions and nodal points not explicitly provided. Our findings have significant implications in the utilization of quantum trajectory simulations. Our approach is instrumental in identifying the optimal control method for generating specific quantum states. Our application of the approach is not limited to continuous-variable quantum systems but can also be applied to more complex quantum systems involving larger or even infinite numbers of variables. Our approach is adaptable to systems where phase transitions occur and where the function's starting point is unclear. Our approach is backed by mathematical analysis, proving its validity and providing essential guidance for its effective use. Our approach is supported by numerical simulations, which validate our analytical claims and showcase its performance. Our approach is offered as a user-friendly, open-source Python package named through-inv, which can be easily integrated into existing code to solve or test inverse problems. Our approach is not just applicable to function inversion but can also be applied to solve inverse problems of constrained optimization, cost-effectiveness analysis, or any type of functional optimization, including the famous NP issue. Our approach is not just applicable to static functions but also to functions with time variability, including the issue of recovering a time-dependent function from a known trajectory. Our approach is not just theoretical but also has significant practical applications, including the performance monitoring and improvement of real-world devices. This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset focusing on driving scenario insights. The dataset contains 21 comprehensive scenario categories, each encompassing 25 distinct scenarios, totaling 425 unique categories. The data was collected from 529 drivers via 15 prominent scenario-based interventions and spans 15,160 miles of naturalistic driving footage, collected over 82 days. The dataset was collected on a major highway in Tucson, Arizona, and the scenario responses were recorded from drivers using a custom-designed instrument. The collected data includes extensive audio and video footage, as well as expert-driven coding to facilitate research. The SceNDD dataset is accessible at: \url{https://github.com/yilunzuo/SceNDD}. Our study also includes a range of innovative applications, showing the potential uses of this dataset, and ultimately outlines future research directions based on its implementation. The research demonstrates that the SceNDD dataset significantly enhances the understanding of driver behavior in various scenario categories and is particularly useful for modeling driver interactions in different situations. Ultimately, the scenario-based insights derived from SceNDD are expected to contribute significantly to the advancement of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems and the development of more realistic simulation environments in the future. The research reveals that the incorporation of scenario information has a profound impact on the predictive accuracy of models, achieving A5cF1 scores of 83.44% and 80.79% for respectively 1s and 5s forecasting on the same highway. Moreover, the scenario-based encoding method significantly improves the realism of simulations, leading to a 36.73% decrease in the average age of vehicles involved in the SceNDD dataset. By utilizing SceNDD, the research was able to explain this simulation result, showing that the majority of simulated crashes occurred when drivers failed to yield to oncoming traffic at intersections. Furthermore, the SceNDD dataset was leveraged to assess the impact of a failed driver yield on the attention allocation to other critical highway features, such as pedestrians crossing the road. The research also explored the potential applications of SceNDD in other fields, such as estimating driver fatigue levels. By applying knowledge discovered from SceNDD, the problem of fatigue was redefined as the driver's failure to comply with the speed limit due to loss of attention. Ultimately, the SceNDD dataset and the accompanying models are expected to contribute significantly to the advancement of future research in the field. The rapid global spread of COVID-19 has prompted countries to adopt a range of measures aimed at slowing its progression. In the absence of a vaccine, many countries have turned to contact tracing as a key strategy for containing the outbreak. Contact tracing technology relies on mobile device data to identify individuals who have come into close contact with someone who has tested positive for the virus. While contact tracing technology is designed to protect public health, its use also raises significant concerns about user privacy. In an effort to mitigate these concerns, contact tracing technology is often promoted as being anonymous, meaning that identifying information about users is not shared with third parties. In this study, we challenge this claim, demonstrating that with minimal additional resources, hackers can reverse-engineer sufficient information about user locations to potentially breach user privacy. Our findings are based on an analysis of the S Saftey Net protocol, which is used in contact tracing COVID-19 applications in several countries, including Brazil. Our research examines the limits of what can be learned about users using Safety Net, as well as ways in which hackers can exploit vulnerabilities in the technology to track users' movements over time. Our ultimate goal is not to highlight the potential risks of contact tracing technology, but rather to leverage our findings to propose improvements to the technology that could help to safeguard user privacy. In particular, we suggest ways in which contact tracing data can be used to identify individuals who have engaged in close contact with someone who has tested positive for the virus, while also preventing unauthorized access to user location data. Our proposed solution aims to strike an appropriate balance between public health goals and individual privacy concerns. Our research was conducted by the N National Cybersecurity Council - Brazil. In our study, we have used a controlled testing environment to assess the security implications of contact tracing technology. Our research looks ahead to exploring these findings in a large scale experimentation to verify the efficiency of the proposed solutions. Our intention is not to share our results publicly at this time, given the potential implications for contact tracing efforts. Our research was funded through a grant from the Funda\c c\~ao de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de S\~ao Paulo. In this paper, we will present our initial findings, which serve as a starting point for a broader set of experimental assessments that we plan to undertake in the future. In the end, we aim to identify ways in which our research can be applied to promote the security and privacy of contact tracing technology. A particular class of functions on $\mathbb{C}^d$ can be expressed as an interaction between linear measurements and complex quantum states. Moreover, these functions possess a specific structure that can be replicated within deep neural networks using complex numbers, despite the networks being agnostic to the quantum nature of the inputs. By employing these networks with quantum data, we gain insights into the required characteristics, establishing a relationship between the tensor ranks of involved operators and the network's complexity. Specifically, we demonstrate that the number of nonlinear operations needed to represent such functions does not exceed $4\cdot{rank}^2$. Utilizing several numerical examples, we investigate the effects of having varying tensor ranks. Ultimately, we discuss the potential implications of our findings on the challenges of analyzing quantum neural networks. These insights might inspire novel approaches to processing quantum information within these networks. Additionally, our work may offer a useful philosophical interpretation of quantum neural networks, providing a bridge between classical deep learning and the unique aspects of quantum computing. The research has also been applied in a different context to neural networks dealing with symbolic inputs in [39]. Our research was initially published as preprints in arXiv in 2019 and 2020, respectively. Formally presenting the results in this thesis allows for a thorough review and presentation of the research before the scientific community. Our research delves into how everyday Signal users, who are not part of the security community, interpret the app's core features. Since these users may not be part of the security realm, we investigate how the app's primary components, particularly the PIN, are perceived. To do this, we gathered 24 Signal users who were not experts and conducted in-depth interviews to understand their views on the app's safety and functionality. The results show that Signal's defenses, intended to shield users against sophisticated attacks, are often viewed as ineffective or confusing. This points to a possibility that users may struggle to grasp even basic security concepts presented within Signal itself. To explore this, we analyzed how the app communicates security-related information and found that users are given both clear and obscure explanations of their actions. We speculate that users receive vague cues because they are not tailored to users' unique circumstances within Signal. Our research highlights the requirement for designers to clarify security features and user benefits, especially when using abstract concepts. Furthermore, our findings suggest that researchers and developers should prioritize user research to better comprehend Signal's defenses and the app's overall user experience. By doing so, developers can address the app's various issues and users can better comprehend and take advantage of the app's features. Ultimately, our study indicates that users are not in a position to take an active role in protecting themselves if they are confused about even basic security components. To enhance user understanding, our recommendations include using simpler and more uniform language to explain security across Signal, refining the app's features to reflect users' comprehension, and providing education and training to help users grasp security concepts. By implementing these suggestions, developers can foster more informed and involved user participation in their security. This study was conducted as part of a larger series that explores the everyday Signal user's comprehension of various components. This research addresses a significant gap within the literature, which has primarily focused on specialists' views. While there are studies on Signal's usability, they have primarily centered on experts' perspectives. By exploring user perceptions that deviate from those of security professionals, our research broadens the understanding of user research. The Signal developers, a non-profit, have given us permission to share this research. Our research is built on 24 interviews, 16 of which are explored in-depth. This has allowed us to gain a deeper understanding of these users' views and develop general recommendations. Complementary research has been conducted via 8 interviews that explore users' thoughts on the app's usability. Our research represents one phase of a larger study. A technical report

The curvature, represented by the Hessian or the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix, plays a crucial role in training neural networks but remains impractical due to its enormous size. Despite its significance, the GGN matrix is often dismissed in training due to computational constraints. However, the ViViT model demonstrates through extensive testing that training with the Hessian is feasible on modern hardware. This is made possible by the 'diminished structure' of the GGN matrix that allows for efficient distributed computing through tensor folding and unfolding operations. These operations enable the vector operations to be performed in a manner similar to that of the Jacobian, thereby taking only 17.5 percent the space required in traditional Hessian storage methods. As a result, it becomes possible to store and compute the Hessian matrix on a device with limited resources. Furthermore, the ViViT model leverages the benefits of the two-parameter solver (TPS) optimizer, known for optimizing models with large models. In line with its innovative optimization technique, the ViViT model achieves state-of-the-art results both in terms of accuracy and efficiency by training the model in a manner that emphasizes network stability. This is made possible by a novel approach to expressing the curvature known as the proximal Hessian, which captures the interdependencies between model parameters through an adjacency matrix that defines a small, optimally-performing sub-network within the larger network. This approach enables the efficient exploration of a stable radius-arm-length profile, where the radius refers to the distance from a model's current optimal state to its nearest local minimum, the arm refers to the distance between different optimisation steps, and the length refers to the total distance between different states in the model. In line with the optimisation technique, the ViViT model achieves superior results on a range of benchmark tests, the results of which surpass current state-of-the-art results by reducing the error rate by 50 percent or increasing the result output by 10 percent in certain cases. This is particularly impressive given that the model is trained using a range of simplified computer programs known as loss functions. Such results validate the potential benefits of training neural networks using the diminished structure of the GGN matrix in a distributed computing environment. This research therefore creates a foundation for the development of future optimized neural network models. These optimized neural network models have the potential to revolutionise a range of application areas including the translation, discovery of the hidden representation in images and the recognition of typed text. We examine this question through the lens of part-of-speech (POS) bias, a concept that evaluates the distinctness of word representations based on POS. We find that in languages that indicate gender, grammatical gender significantly affects POS-based distinctness. Specifically, words from the same POS group with different genders are tended to be treated as separate entities by current language models. We investigate the underlying factors contributing to POS bias and discover that contextual information related to animacy and human intent play a crucial role. We also identify the implications of POS bias resulting from grammatical gender on current AI systems. We observe that models encoding gender information primarily rely on grammatical cues rather than real-world gender associations. We highlight potential consequences of POS bias and recommend future research directions to address these challenges. Predicting future traffic flows is essential for optimal city transportation management.
However, gathering timely and relevant data for this purpose is often costly and time-consuming.
As a result, a significant challenge in traffic analysis is working with scarce, noisy, and irregularly-sampled data.
Typically, researchers focus on forecasting a single point in time, but our study aims to expand this to multiple hours in the near future.
To achieve this, we've defined a novel task known as Sparse Traffic Forecasting.
By applying similarity-driven features from spatio-temporal domains, we've developed an effective solution to STFC.
Our approach features multiple layers of feature extraction that use similarities.
Empirical evaluations on real-world data demonstrate the efficiency of our proposed method.
Moreover, our method won the 2021 AI-Challenge: Sparse Traffic Forecasting competition.

Research into these factors has been extensive, with existing studies primarily focusing on developed markets like the United States. By employing multiple regression analysis, this study confirms that certain film features, like 3D technology and celebrity participation, have a significant correlation with box office profits regardless of the location. Interestingly, while the influence of film attributes on earnings exhibits geographical consistency, the impact of release timing and month significantly varies across different countries. In addition, the study provides policy recommendations tailored to three distinct categories of films: blockbuster, mid-budget, and low-budget films. Notably, this study reveals that low-budget films have greater potential to achieve success in developing countries. Consequently, promoting such films in developing countries and supporting them at their peak in developed countries is expected to yield the most box office profits. CPN2 is an innovative, open-source platform designed for analyzing and simulated management of large, interconnected cyber-physical social networks. This human-driven network model is based on a multi-level, reinforcement-learning system incorporating probabilistic behavior. The system uses a compact data model to facilitate the efficient simulation and analysis of dynamic CPSNs. The introduction of an intelligent, autonomous agent in the CPN2 framework allows for seamless integration of human decision-making into the system. This agent utilizes a complex decision-making process to address uncertainty and conflicts within the system, ultimately providing a comprehensive view of CPSNs that can be utilized for both simulation and analysis purposes. CPN2 is supported by a suite of ready-to-use tools that facilitate the creation of various CPSN scenarios, as well as customized models and simulations. These tools make it possible to study CPSN dynamics and evaluate the effectiveness of different strategies and interventions. The CPN2 framework can be applied to a wide range of CPSN applications, including public health, environment protection, transportation systems, and critical cyber-physical infrastructure, with ongoing development focused on expanding the toolset and applying CPN2 to new use cases. Blazars exhibit spectral features that include X-ray/UV bumps, an UV/soft X-ray bump, and a curious excess in the UV/soft X-ray range. Initially, this excess was attributed to radiative cooling but this model has its limitations. A different approach, partially polarized inverse external Compton scattering (PIS) of the black hole's shadow on the accretion disk, is now being considered as a possible alternative explanation for the excess. When applied to six blazars and six Fermi blazars, a PIS contribution was detected in every case at higher frequencies than the usual cooling model. This concept has led to a range of interesting ideas, including methods to analyze quantum states in an intrinsic way, to identify whether states are orthogonal, and to recognize symmetric states within general states. Here, we focus on the digital verification of symmetric pure states. By utilizing standard procedures from digital image processing, we can confirm that a pure state is symmetric if its corresponding image satisfies certain conditions regarding digital symmetry and parity. Additionally, we explore the requirements necessary for the proposed methods to be reliable in quantum systems. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of identifying symmetric pure states in a Bell state space by employing basic principles from quantum mechanics. This approach involves expanding quantum vectors into eigenfunction expansions and applying image processing techniques based on the associated eigenfunctions. Experimental realizations of these concepts could lead to innovative applications in fields such as quantum communication and quantum computing. This research may also inspire other interesting connections between quantum mechanics and image processing. A novel approach to baryon formation is suggested in a context of a rapidly changing quantum environment. Baryons originate not just from colour-neutral quantum fragments produced by colour field proliferation, but also from quantized fusion processes of colour charges accumulated within enstrophy-rich QCD filaments. This new concept is centered on a rapidly developing, helical QCD filament forming pattern, where we calculate the rate of colour charge transfer along the filament's spiral axis. The resulting prediction is that baryons are created in proportion to the enstrophy generated, a quantity characterizing the complexity of this pattern's configuration space. This proportionality bridges the microscopic level (enstrophy production) and the manifestation of baryon formation at a hadronisation instant. Additionally, we offer a theoretical explanation for a phenomenon, previously observed in [arXiv:2109.04422], where an positive correlation exists between baryon production and energy concentration (enstrophy) in helical QCD filaments. Importantly, the former's origin is not rooted in the local energy level of these filaments but rather in their geometric properties (helicity). This new model is further validated by demonstrating its applicability to an extended case of right-handed and left-handed spiral patterns. Eventually, the theoretical framework is extended to a general case of arbitrary helicity observed in systems (e.g., turbulence, vortical beams). Depending on the degree of rotation helicity can either positively or negatively correlate with baryon production. The research is accompanied by the creation of visual aids illustrating baryon generation in a rapidly developing, helical QCD filament. The associated movie can be found through the link, [supplementary material (arXiv:2102.04959)]. The research offered in the paper has been conducted as part of a broader project aimed at developing a quantum mechanical theory of baryon formation, efforts that are described in detail by arXiv:2102.04959. This fundamental concept is part of a broader project whose goal is to break down baryons into elementary colour charge accumulations, a process discussed earlier in arXiv:2009.04398. In the study of the sun's internal rotation, helioseismic analysis relies on measuring the travel time of seismic waves across different distances on the sun's surface. However, the traditional method used to calculate these travel times may have a systematic error due to a side-to-side movement of active regions across the sun's surface over time. This movement causes a systematic error in travel time measurements in the north-south direction, which needs to be corrected. An unbiased estimate of this error was calculated for the period between 1996 and 2014. The study found that the error is about 0.15 seconds for the 2-6.5 degrees latitude range and 0.25 seconds for the 6.5-10 degrees latitude range. An empirical formula to calculate the error based on the latitude and time period is provided. Additionally, the study found that the error is dominated by the movement of the sun's sunspots rather than other types of magnetic regions. This finding is based on the analysis of historical sunspot data. An empirical formula to calculate the error based on the ratio of moving active regions to total active regions is provided. The study also found that the error is affected by the movement of equatorial beta pseudorapidity jets, which are regions on the sun's surface identified by specific patterns. An empirical formula to calculate the error based on the movement of these jets is provided. The study suggests that the error needs to be corrected for the 1995-2014 period and most likely needs to be corrected for other time periods as well. As a result, the error needs to be addressed before it affects the sun's internal rotation research. An empirical correction formula is provided and it's recommended to use this formula until a more accurate analysis is conducted. Moreover, the error affects the sun's internal rotation research rather than the sun's oscillation frequency measurements. Finally, the study provides recommendations for future research which should utilize the correct data and avoid introducing systematic errors. An example of this is the bridge feature research, which should utilize the correct data and avoid the systematic errors. An empirical feature extraction method is provided and it's recommended to use this method for the 1995-2014 period and similar methods for other time periods. The study also provides recommendations for the research of sun's internal rotation based on the sun's velocity maps and specific signs that indicate the sun's rotational movement. This wave amplitude is linked to a phenomenon where cosmic string loops produce oscillations due to the non-uniform distribution of electromagnetic forces during the loop's breaking process. Adjusting the model's parameters allows for compatibility with both gravitational wave and electromagnetic data. Moreover, the wave spectrum exhibits a peak near a frequency of 1.035 times the gravitational wave period of the GW170817 event, caused by loop scaling oscillations that align with the expectation for waves produced by binary black hole mergers. This alignment with expectations is distinct from the scenario where waves are produced by the primary acoustic peak due to inflationary perturbations. Our results reveal that pulsar timing arrays offer a unique opportunity to obtain insights into the dynamics of high-frequency gravitational waves and the characteristics of high-energy electromagnetic fields in the early universe. This insight offers a powerful tool for studying the interaction between gravity, light, and electromagnetic forces at the quantum level through the loop's breaking process, with the tool being distinguishable due to its unique gravitational wave properties. These include a monochromatic rather than broadband spectrum, a peak in gravitational waves in the 1.05 frequency band of pulsar timing, and a connection between electromagnetic loops breaking through photon-electron interaction in stars and the gravitational waves detected by the GW170817 event. The tool is further applied to the gravitational waves detected by the LIGO-Virgo Collaborations from the primary acoustic peaks produced by inflationary perturbations, where the analysis reveals a conflict with the results from pulsar timing arrays. This conflict is resolved by assuming a secondary frequency produced by the electromagnetic loops breaking in the gravitational wave spectrum at the LIGO-Virgo frequency band, where the results show a small ratio of order 0.05 between the secondary and primary frequencies. This ratio of frequencies has implications for the electric field of quantum gravitational waves at the quantum level through the Big-Ratio for stars, with the B-Ratio regulating a critical feature in the high-energy spectrum of quantum gravitational waves produced by electromagnetic loops breaking in the LIGO-Virgo frequency band at the stellar level through the gravitational wave photon interaction in stars. This feature regulates a critical mass at the stellar surface that separates the high and low energy spectra of quantum gravitational waves produced by electromagnetic loops breaking in the LIGO-Virgo frequency band at the stellar surface through the gravitational wave photon interaction in stars.

Achieving effective Cross-Lingual Information Retrieval (CLIR) where queries can be formulated in any language is a significant challenge. Traditional approaches rely on translating queries into the target language, but often fail to meet the monolingual baseline. To overcome this limitation, emerging research turns to leveraging source-language queries and exploits contextual information to enhance CLIR performance. Both interactive and non-interactive frameworks have been explored for building retrieval models that utilize contextual information. The former demands human participation via data annotation, whereas the latter doesn't require human involvement.

While both frameworks have been explored individually, their potential for joint exploration and adaptation remains uninvestigated. In this work, we treat the annotation process as a training task, incorporating an interactive module that takes advantage of contextual signals from annotated data. By providing query-answer pairs and allowing the system to make predictions, humans can obtain further guidance, and the system can refine its understanding of contextual information. This human-system interaction not only boosts data quality through active learning but also enables the system to tap into additional contextual signals in unannotated data. The back-and-forth between human and system allows human-generated signals to be utilized for enhancing CLIR models in both interactive and non-interactive settings. Experiments on six datasets from Wikipedia and Wikidata reveal that our two-framework approach outperforms the baseline by 8.2%. The code and data are available on GitHub. Furthermore, through ablation studies, we found that human participation has limited impact on performance, and most of the improvement stems from the shared benefits of human-system interaction. The significant boost in performance over the non-interactive framework confirms the value of incorporating contextual information. Interestingly, our two-framework approach still outperforms the baseline even when excluding vector-based retrieval, suggesting that the proposed method can effectively extract and harness various types of contextual information. Finally, our analysis of error statistics highlights that the majority of misfires occur due to the lack of explicit representation for numerical and special tokens, underscoring the importance of comprehensive token representation in CLIR. The paper discusses limitations, potential extensions, and offers insights for the reader. The token-based analysis also motivates the development of new tokens for enhanced performance. Importantly, this work not only contributes to CLIR but also sheds light on the application of human-system interaction in other natural language processing tasks. The behavioral understanding of contextual information in CLIR can serve as a starting point for similar research in other domains. The paper explores the conditions under which human-system interaction benefits CLIR models and identifies ways to maximize this

Our results show that the core's formation is divided into two phases: the free fall phase and the ambipolar diffusion phase. During the free fall phase, the core's midplane becomes extremely cold due to the lack of ambipolar diffusion, while larger scales remain at equilibrium temperatures. As ambipolar diffusion sets in, a layered structure develops, with polar layers being more transparent than the midplane. Dust particles can easily settle toward the midplane, regaining the core's initial properties. During the night of October 10, 2019, the Large Binocular Telescope found itself shadowed by the moon from its usual target, allowing for a unique observation of the atmosphere above Tucson, Arizona. By comparing on-sky observations with those from both a simple atmospheric model and a more complex simulation, we found both models failed to perfectly replicate the behavior of the actual atmosphere. By matching the simple model to the observed data, we set an upper limit on the variation in atmospheric motion, limiting it to a maximum of 10% change in atmospheric flow. This limit holds until a 10-minute time frame, after which it becomes necessary to use the more complex simulation model to accurately predict the behavior of the atmosphere. Applying this approach to the observation of a reference star, we found the large binocular telescope was able to maintain a stable lock on the star for 8 minutes and 31 seconds before switching to the more complex simulation model. This study provides essential insights for characterizing the atmosphere above observatories and determining when either of the two models should be used to accurately predict the behavior of the atmosphere during astronomical observations. Moreover, this approach can be applied to a wide range of Observatories and atmospheric models and is not limited to the specific setup of the large binocular telescope. An accompanying video shows the observed atmosphere in motion above the observatory and displays the difference between the simple and atmospheric model simulation. This research has been further discussed in a follow-up article where we explore the potential to use the large binocular telescope to study the lower atmosphere on other planets, including Mars. This follow-up study relies on the understanding of the atmosphere behavior that we derived in this article and allows us to make predictions about the observed atmosphere behavior on other planets. Time series forecasting has become an essential component of modern business and finance, with significant applications in stock market predictions, supply demand estimates, and commodity price estimates. The key challenge here is accounting for the complexities of time series, including its inherent irregularity and the need for modeling across multiple time points. By treating each time step as a probability distribution centered on an underlying trend, the issues of irregular time intervals and multi-step forecasting can be effectively addressed. To achieve this, we develop a novel statistical model, incorporating a key constraint that eliminates unnecessary density in time, allowing for significant improvements over existing methods. The efficacy of our model is demonstrated through comparisons with leading approaches on a range of empirical datasets. Federated learning allows a central server to coordinate a collaborative machine learning model across multiple devices while keeping user data confidential by not sharing it with the server. Although this model preserves users' data privacy, the server does control the training process. Our research investigates how the server can ensure that the trained model is equitable and private for all participants, and we explore existing and proposed methods for achieving this, including a new technique from one of our studies that relies on differential privacy. We've tested these methods in a federated learning context for training a model to predict students' academic performance based on demographic and performance data, with the goal of ensuring that the model doesn't make biased predictions based on the data it receives from participating schools. Ultimately, we've found that a combination of several techniques is necessary to ensure that the trained model is equitable and private. Our analysis highlights the trade-offs between equity, privacy, and accuracy, and provides an understanding of the effectiveness of various techniques in different contexts. Our research has implications not only for the responsible development of machine learning models but also for the general principles of decision-making, as our findings relate to the interplay between bias, privacy, and accuracy. Our methods are available in open-source form at https://github.com/usace/responsible-ml. Moreover, our research demonstrates that a participating school can mitigate the bias in the trained model by strategically which data is sent to the server. Our study also demonstrates that several existing methods for achieving equity can be challenging to use in practice due to requirements such as the need for a training dataset, the need to trust a model, or the need to modify the training process. This research centers on enhancing end-to-end transmission efficiency in a wireless energy transfer network assisted by intelligent surfaces (ISs). The challenge is to find the optimal reflection strategy for ISs and data transmission settings at the transmitter, including power levels and information rates, for each state of the transmitter's battery. The system operates within a specific time frame with discrete time slots where the transmitter continuously charges the receiver until the receiver reaches full energy capacity and then sends data for a specified time before once again the charging process begins. The problem is cast to find the optimal number of IS virtual tags to use in machine learning through loss function optimization while considering the receiver's battery state and its impact on IS reflection and data transmission. A deep learning model is developed for ISs and data transmission optimization, where a neural network is trained on sampled values of IS positions to predict the best reflection strategy for maximum data transfer speed given any receiver battery state. The model also includes a neural network trained through loss function optimization to set data transmission parameters to maximize data transfer speed. The results show that our proposed approach outperforms other optimized methods by 25% to 81%. Additionally, our method requires significantly less training time and effort compared to sampling-based methods. It's also shown that our model can handle variations in IS shape and size and malfunctions as well as continues to function effectively even if the receiver's battery is fully drained. However, RN-based GANs still struggle to improve existing state-of-the-art models in producing high-quality image generation. To address this limitation, our research introduces a new triplet-based RN GAN approach, aiming to produce photo-realistic images through improved discriminator training. By combining RN and triplet loss, our approach enables the RN discriminator to accurately distinguish real and fake images, leading to improved discriminator performance and higher quality image generation. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our RN GAN achieves state-of-the-art results on both ImageNet and FFHQ datasets, outperforming existing GANs in terms of both image generation and discriminator performance. Notably, our approach produces photo-realistic images that surpass previous studies, providing valuable insights for the field of image generation. One critical factor determining the success of neural architecture search lies in mitigating interference between diverse design options within the search space. To grasp this challenge, we conduct in-depth analysis across three prominent NAS benchmarks to identify the characteristics of design interference, coupled with an efficient yet highly robust controller, that can effectively navigate this obstacle. Through our investigation, we establish that the controller learns task-specific differences via abstract symmetries, which however breaks down when dealing with high-resolution vision tasks. To tackle this issue, we introduce the i2c controller that employs latent representation clustering, thereby enhancing its task-invariance and achieving better test results with reduced computational cost, spanning 2 to 10 times, depending on the task. Notably, the computational savings on the SNAS benchmark of designing an ResNet 56 model is remarkably high, amounting to 8.75 times. Inspired by the insight that different architecture designs focus on distinct subset patterns, we propose a controller that optimally allocates resources within each subset. Specifically, we propose the i2c CDC controller that clusters the latent representation, and employs a controller that allocates resources within each subset. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed architecture design approaches. For instance, the architecture designs obtained from our method yield a 1.3 point improvement over CDC in terms of the validation accuracy on the SNAS benchmark of designing an ResNet 56 model, with 8.75 times less computational cost. Moreover, a model designed by our method reaches an accuracy of 50.2 point on the SNAS benchmark of designing an ResNet 220 model, surpassing the state-of-the-art model designed by SNAS with an accuracy of 49.4 point. Videos demonstrating the controller's behavior are available at: https://youtu.be/2kQpS8kH0O0. This article expands upon the conference paper by J. Z. Chen et al., with the significant additions including the following: 1) An optimized controller design inspired by the insight that different architecture designs focus on distinct subset patterns. 2) A systematic approach to investigating the characteristics of design interference. 3) A rigorous evaluation of the controller's ability to handle the interference by conducting the analysis across three prominent NAS benchmarks. 4) An empirical analysis of the impact of design interference. 5) An empirical analysis of the impact of contamination. 6) An analysis of the impact of summary contamination. 7) An analysis of the impact of the number of samples on the controller's behavior.

Time-series analysis, a broad category, encompasses examining individual data points across various dimensions over time and detecting unusual occurrences in continuous flows of data.  Key time-series attributes include measurement scale, study period, and geographic location.  This work presents a generic framework for R code that can handle any time-series measurement and duration, and is suitable for discoveries spanning seconds to years.  The framework supports discoveries involving a single data point or multiple points, as well as separate analyses for each, and we provide examples of detecting unusual occurrences in such data.  Ultimately, this framework is a versatile tool that can be applied to a wide range of time-series data.

We demonstrate that in a $CAT(0)$ space with all geodesic completeness, the non-trivial edges of the 1-skeleton are specifically those of right-angled Artin groups. Furthermore, our proof reveals an algorithm to automatically identify and check if a given group meets these criteria, involving a repeated process of forming and analyzing a new group derived from modified tree coverings. Additionally, our findings also yield an alternative proof of a previously established result, showing that groups with the $CAT(0)$ structure and featuring only edge-transitive 1-skeletons are essentially right-angled Artin groups. Notably, our study shows that not all right-angled Artin groups satisfy the criteria of having all geodesic complete 1-skeletons, leading to the introduction of a new class of right-angled Artin groups termed "edge-transitive". The anticipated value of a lottery ticket represents the expected sum of its future values, which varies according to the draw of $N$ numbers from $M$ options in each round. The ticket's value at each draw is a random function $X_n$ and the sum of two components after $T-1$ draws is maximized by optimizing the buying time. One component is a fixed payment $\tau \ge 0$, which is known beforehand, while the other is a random bonus $\sigma \ge 0$. Assuming that for every $n \le T-1$, the random function $X_n$ and the draw parameters satisfy certain general conditions, which are widely applicable in practice, our goal is to determine the optimal time $t^*$ to purchase the ticket that maximizes the sum of these two components. An explicit expression for $t^*$ is derived through dynamic programming and it is shown that it is the optimal solution. Furthermore, our results are verified and validated using real data from the lotteries in Israel. In addition, our research has significant practical implications by offering insights on how and when to market such a lottery ticket effectively in a real-world scenario. The number of possible options for the optimal time to purchase the lottery ticket is highly dependent on these parameters, which indicates that marketing strategies should take them into consideration, in order to identify the best stage to market the lottery ticket. t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on noninformative noise in the data, which isn't necessarily true for datasets with inherent structure like directional data on a sphere. Current implementations of t-SNE rely on the Gaussian distribution to model such data, but this leads to significant losses due to the constraint-based nature of the data. We introduce a novel, spherical version of t-SNE that leverages the von Mises-Fisher distribution, offering a more efficient and accurate alternative. This new approach exploits the data's spherical structure, using the VMF model to minimize both artificial noise and data distortion. We provide a detailed description, evaluate its performance in comparison to existing methods, and showcase its practical applications. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/cchange/vmf-t-SNE. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that VMF-SNE produces more accurate visualizations than its Gaussian counterpart. Moreover, in the context of point-cloud clustering, our approach achieves a higher rate of correct segmentation. In this paper, we establish "steadfast homology." A chromatic alpha structure defines this homology. Our study focuses on the core module of this structure, using which we can define the steadfast homology. We demonstrate that it forms a module steady in chromatic terms. Furthermore, we establish that the steadfast homology of an enriched chromatic alpha structure is a vector of its classical Alexander module's stable locus. Additionally, we show that the steadfast homology of a chromatic alpha structure enriched over another module is the stable locus of the combined object's classical Alexander module. These findings have significant implications for the study of Alexander modules in general, leading to a key theorem. The theorem states that the stable Alexander module of any finitely generated group with a single relator is steady in chromatic terms. We then extend this analysis to the study of classical Alexander modules' singularities via the application of steadfast homology. Notably, we show that the steadfast homology of the Alexander module for the complement of an A_n singular point is a module steady in chromatic terms that is invariant under the action of the group. Similarly, we establish that the steadfast homology of the combined object for the L-space constructed from the link of the Clifford torus is a module steady in chromatic terms. In fact, we show that the steadfast homology of the combined object for any L-space is stable. Using the red, green, and blue formalism, we can define the steadfast homology of the combined object for the complement of a torus knot. In particular, we demonstrate that the steadfast homology of the combined object for the regular torus knot is defined by the vector [1, 1-2p]. In fact, we can extend this analysis to the study of the stellar homology of torus links via the application of a chromatic alpha structure enriched over another module. Notably, we show that the stellar homology of the combined object for the regular torus knot is stable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the stellar homology of the combined object for the L-space constructed from the link of the Clifford torus is stable. In fact, we can extend this analysis to the study of the stellar homology of any L-space. Finally, we can extend the analysis of the red, green, and blue formalism to the study of the stellar homology of the complement of an A_n singular point. This work showcases a critical aspect of dynamic power management in multi-user interference networks through the analysis of generalized degrees of freedom. Optimally managing power in line with channel conditions can significantly improve network performance, however this comes at a significant cost due to the need for precise channel measurements. Introducing noise into these measurements reduces the effectiveness of optimal power management, instead of providing any benefit below a certain noise threshold. By comparing optimal and binary (two-level) power management, we find that the extent to which optimal management outperforms binary in terms of GFDoG is proportional to the square root of the number of users. This result holds regardless of whether the binary power level is set to 0 or 1. Moreover, we identify the maximum possible GFDoG gain achieved using binary rather than optimal power management. Our analysis reveals that the optimal power management gain is a valuable tool for determining the achievable GFDoG limits in various network scenarios including single-user, multi-level and fully connected topologies. In addition to its relevance to power management, our work also shows that the power management gap can be leveraged to enhance direct and reverse compute-and-forward operations in general RF and molecular communication networks. Finally, we demonstrate the power management's influence on the GFDoG capacity-mass tradeoff in molecular communication networks. [Abstract]
