This research aims to improve the accuracy and robustness of pose graph optimization by addressing the issue of bias against certain vehicle configurations in lidar point matching. An end-to-end deep neural network (DNN) filter is proposed to detect and correct bias across various vehicle shapes. The proposed DNN filter can effectively work with existing lidar matching algorithms without needing modification and is applicable in a variety of settings. An experimental setup featuring vehicles with distinct designs such as cars, trucks, and vans in urban and highway environments is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the DNN filter. Furthermore, we show that the proposed DNN filter can accurately detect and correct bias even for vehicles that have not been included in its training dataset. Additionally, we investigate the impact of bias variation on the effectiveness of the DNN filter and explore the potential causes of bias variation and how to address them through training a more comprehensive DNN filter. An investigation of the potential trade-offs between the level of detail in the DNN filter's feature maps and pose error optimization is also conducted. Finally, we examine the effect of the proposed DNN filter on high-level tasks such as localization in self-driving cars. An additional study was conducted to verify that the DNN filter does not introduce bias against previously unseen vehicle configurations. We collected a new dataset, dubbed prejudice-misaligned-urban, which features the alignment of lidar data collected by a vehicle with a unique design, along with urban coverage and misaligned lidar data. The DNN filter was trained on the new dataset while assuming that the bias does not exist for the studied vehicle configuration and as a result, the DNN filter generalizes poorly on the urban coverage and misaligned lidar data. Moreover, the DNN filter was trained on the new dataset while assuming that the bias does not exist for the studied vehicle configuration and as a result, the DNN filter does not rectify the alignment of the vehicle with a unique design, indicating the absence of bias. These studies highlight the importance of including various vehicle configurations in the training dataset of the DNN filter. An investigation of the effect of the DNN filter training dataset composition on the effectiveness of the DNN filter was conducted in a previous study. An additional study was conducted to investigate the relationship between the complexity of the DNN filter and the requirement for the training dataset. Extracting information from high-resolution satellite images has become essential 
for numerous applications, leading many researchers to leverage powerful yet 
resource-intensive deep learning methods. These techniques primarily focus on 
resolving specific tasks rather than addressing the broader requirements of 
satellite imagery. To address this, our study develops a comprehensive framework 
aimed at identifying and extracting detailed edge information from these images, 
utilizing established image processing techniques. We draw inspiration from a 
production pipeline utilized in space exploration applications, incorporating an 
enhanced version of the Canny edge detection algorithm paired with an adaptive 
thresholding method based on the Sobel edge operator. We evaluate our proposed 
method against contemporary deep learning approaches, incorporating performance 
metrics commonly used in satellite image processing, and conduct an extensive 
analysis of edge detection across diverse applications. Furthermore, our study 
illustrates the significance of edge information in enhancing the detection and 
identification of complex objects within space exploration contexts. To support 
other researchers, our team makes the source code for this analysis available 
on GitHub, alongside all necessary datasets. We hope this work facilitates a 
better understanding of edge detection and contributes to the development of 
more efficient methods for extracting information from satellite images. By 
demonstrating that deep learning is not the sole solution for working with 
satellite imagery, our study encourages future research in this field. Lastly, we 
hope this tutorial provides valuable insights for professionals and students to 
explore image processing techniques as a valuable starting point for working with

In the study of X-ray absorption, the rate of photon absorption is influenced by the rates at which electrons are created and how ions transition between states. The advanced rate equation model presented here expands upon the electron population distribution to describe this process, offering a unified framework that can generate both linear and non-linear absorption spectra. The models' consistency with the principles of quantum mechanics and their respective mathematical formulations are discussed. The rate equation model is formulated as a first-order linear system of ordinary differential equations, requiring the determination of four key rates. We provide conditions to establish that this system is well-behng and has a unique solution. Furthermore, we offer an analytical method to calculate the population distribution using the Laplace transform. The models were tested using numerical examples of both a one- and two-energy-level system, compared with the Monte Carlo method, and were found to accurately account for the effects of both photoionization and recombination. The rate equation model was also used to create a graphical user interface that generates X-ray absorption near edge structure spectra. The model was found to accurately account for non-linear effects that arise when x-ray flux is high. The flux required to produce non-linear effects is heavily dependent on the speed of absorption and emission. The rate equation model was designed with the intention of facilitating machine learning research, allowing the learning of laws related to electron transitions from data. We also discuss how this model can be extended to investigate other phenomena. The model's code is available under a free software license at https://github.com/aseaton/Rate-Equation-XAS. Support vector machines have proven effective in a range of applications, including in machine learning. A key aspect of support vector machines is their use of a kernel trick to execute learning. In our study, we investigate the application of GAN in generating kernels for categorizing amplitude shift keying signals. Specifically, we explore the category prediction accuracy of amplitude shift keying signals generated by waveGAN and waveunet GAN in relation to support vector machine classification. Notably, we find that a combination, or blend, of waveGAN and waveunet GAN improves predictive accuracy and provides resilience against adversarial assaults. This research has significant implications for professional communication in a hostile environment. Moreover, we contribute to the existing literature by adapting machine learning techniques originally designed for images and speech to the realm of radio signals. Our findings suggest that radio signal categorization can be performed with high accuracy using support vector machine classification on amplitude shift keying signals generated by the blend of waveGAN and waveunet GAN. This approach achieves high accuracy, specifically 99.8%, for F1 scores in our experimental setup. Furthermore, the precision and recall of our method demonstrate consistent patterns. Interestingly, the performance of waveunet GAN surpasses that of waveGAN, indicating that GAN architecture enhances predictive accuracy. This distinction highlights the importance of architecture design when applying the kernel trick to amplitude shift keying signals. Our study also assesses the first-order and second-order adversarial assaults against the supported vector machine classifier. Interestingly, the assault on the blend of waveGAN and waveunet GAN reduces classification accuracy from 99.8% to 20.16%. In contrast, the same assault lowers classification accuracy of waveunet GAN from 99.8% to 98.505%. This distinction underscores the robustness of the blend of waveGAN and waveunet GAN under adversarial assaults. Moreover, the classification accuracy of waveunet GAN and waveGAN exceeds that of a ten-layer convolutional network in our previous study. Our study further evaluates the robustness of the blend of waveGAN and waveunet GAN using a second-order assault. This assault on the blend of waveGAN and waveunet GAN reduces classification accuracy from 99.8% to 20.16%. Consequently, the blend of waveGAN and waveunet GAN displays strong resilience against second-order adversarial assaults. Automated multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation faces the challenge of inconsistent performance across different datasets and clinics due to variations in data quality. To address this issue, many MS segmentation models are retrained in each individual clinic using the paper's first scenario. However, this approach can be impractical and inefficient, particularly given the growing availability of MS datasets. The paper explores alternative solutions by combining data from multiple sources through the domain adaptation framework. The second scenario considers using a single, comprehensive dataset to train a base model, which can then be fine-tuned at various clinics. While both approaches have potential, they face unique challenges: domain adaptation typically sees performance decline in subsequent adaptations, while models trained on a base dataset may not adapt as effectively to new clinics. Ultimately, the paper recommends continuous learning without data regeneration as the most balanced strategy. To implement this, the paper proposes a straightforward continuation multi-domain adaptation approach and complements it with different network architectures. The methods' effectiveness are evaluated through lesion segmentation using third-party code on two public datasets and a synthetic dataset simulating the differences between datasets. The results indicate that domain adaptation leads to a loss of performance across subsequent adaptations, while network continuation without data regeneration offers the most balanced trade-off and is thus the preferred choice. The research also identifies the need to adjust architecture to mitigate adaptation challenges and observes that domain adaptation performance is largely dependent on the balance between adapting to local details and maintaining overall representation. To address this, the paper introduces a multi-domain continuation architecture that enhances the generalization of local features to different domain adaptations. Evaluations on public datasets and a synthetic dataset reveal the potential of this approach to improve domain adaptation performance. Ultimately, the research recommends network continuation without data regeneration and offers novel architecture design to enhance domain adaptation. The presence of Infrared Dark Nebulae (IDNs) serves as testimony to the formation of massive stars.  Among the observed candidates, those associated with the core of the Dragon IDN exhibit the most pronounced signs of massive star formation.  The spectrum obtained from the Spitzer space telescope reveals the characteristic emission of ions such as [O I], [S III], and other features, in addition to the PAH and C IV lines that suggest the generation of ultraviolet radiation.  The absence of a companion star in this region positions it perfectly for the formation of a massive, ultra-compact star through the process of core collapse.  Furthermore, the light curve analysis of this IDN displays a predictable variability pattern that is linked to the rotation of the sheath, rather than being influenced by the movement of the core itself, providing insight into its structure.  The sheath's density is significantly higher near the edge but the core itself does not exhibit such characteristics and instead appears to be enveloped within it.  The derived core and sheath properties provide valuable insights into the core's evolution, and suggest that the ultraviolet radiation from the massive star is likely to stimulate further formation, and that the formation of a second massive star is a real possibility.  The presence of IDNs such as the Dragon's core serves as a reminder that massive star formation can occur through both core collapse and disk fragmentation, and that IDNs are pivotal in understanding this process.  The widespread presence of these nebulae in various star forming environments also means that the massive star formation pathway associated with IDNs is likely to be more widespread than currently understood.  The further observation of the physical structure and movement of the core in the Dragon IDN through the imaging data from the James Webb telescope will provide significant insight into its development.  The discovery of this IDN, and its potential to give rise to multiple massive stars through the process of core collapse, presents significant hope for the detection of similar formations across the universe.  The presence of other IDNs also holds out this possibility, and further research could lead to the identification of the basic pathway to massive star formation.  However, and more importantly, the widespread occurrence of IDNs across various star forming environments also raises serious concerns, as they provide a prime location for the formation of runaway massive star collisions that could lead to the disruption of developing planetary systems, and further research is needed to understand the role of IDNs in the galaxy. To address the problem of preferential comparisons among collections, we created the taut Logical Preference Ordering, and then developed the contextually inclusive variant, LCPO, by integrating taut logical preferences into Tarskian bivaluations. LCPO represents a pioneering application of contextual reasoning in social choice theory and decision theory. Building on LCPO, we introduced the non-contextual version, LCPOcc, by imposing specific conditions on individual preferences. We found that LCPOcc adheres to seven fundamental properties of preference orderings. Through the use of an example with three elemental sets, A, B, and C, we illustrated how different social choices can be made, either individually or collectively, depending on the presence of A, B, and C. While an individual with the non-contextual preference ordering, LCPOcc, prefers A over B, a group with the same preferences prefers to add only C. This distinction between individual and collective preferences, along with the ability to add unique or common elements, allows us to analyze the phenomenon from two perspectives: a comprehensive, monadic approach that focuses on individual preferences, and a more nuanced, binary perspective that considers the interactions between individual preferences and the added elements. We observed that LCPOcc's behavior under the binary perspective satisfies seven properties similar to those found in single-preference approaches. Nonetheless, our results show that LCPOcc fails to meet all seven requirements when applied to the monadic perspective. Ultimately, we propose that the binary approach offers a more robust model for analyzing preference orderings, especially when dealing with the addition of collections. Moreover, our results indicate that binary perspectives possess inherent qualities that enable consistent decision-making, whereas monadic approaches may lead to contradictions. In light of this, we suggest that the binary perspective should be the preferred model for studying set addition problems. Furthermore, our work on LCPO has significantly advanced the frontiers of contextual reasoning in social choice theory and decision-making, embodying a groundbreaking application of contextual reasoning in these fields. In contrast, the ability of binary models to produce consistent results makes them well-suited for practical applications, as demonstrated by their widespread use in voting systems. In line with this, our study of LCPO has identified a promising area for further research, while our results on binary models have implications for both theoretical and practical contexts. The properties identified in this paper can serve as a starting point for exploring other preference models, set addition problems, or collection-based comparisons. In the final stages of neural machine translation decoding, a key objective is to generate a well-formed output produced close in time to relevant context. Yet, traditional models focus on past production history. We propose the Look-forward Attention (LFA) module, which incorporates future production history in computation. By using an adapted relative position vector in LFA, the normally limited attention mechanism in neural machine translation is able to look ahead and consider non-neighboring words in the target sequence. Our experiments on the standard IWSLT datasets demonstrate significant improvements, with gains of over 2 BLEU points for the large model variant on the English-to-Chinese task when incorporating 5 additional look-forward steps out of a total of 30 decoding steps. Notably, the improvements are most pronounced when decoding is far from its end, and the spatial structure of the model allows for reduced minimum BLEU score variability at the final decoding step. Furthermore, using LFA in conjunction with NMT displacement features leads to improved translation quality. The code for our model is available at https://github.com/kenresearch17/Look-forward_Attention.

We have derived a precise large N expression for the thermal entropy of a specific large N CFT on a 2-dimensional plane with a specific type of scalar field connection. The connection's non-linearity is characterized by an algebraic function with parameters a and b. The entropy we found matches a known combinatorial formula for a type of holomorphic vortex lattice, confirming a previous hypothesis. Conversely, we obtained a large N expression for the entanglement entropy of a different region within the same CFT and found it leads to a known phase transition when the parameters are changed, resulting in a non-intuitive ground state. The ground state shows negative entropy in a type of CFT that models a 2-dimensional black hole, pointing out a distinction between thermal and entanglement entropies. Additionally, we obtained a large N expression for the entanglement entropy of a strip region in a CFT with a specific type of scalar field connection, and the results show parameter-dependent periodicity. Cai, Song and Kou had a significant breakthrough in 2015 with their paper "A Feynman-Kac Representation of Generalized PDEs of Volterra Type". Their work was further developed in 2017 through the paper "Stochastic Partial SDEs for Reversible Jump Diffusions and Their Potential Applications". These applications included a special case of pricing Asian options with a stochastic volatility. In 2018, another paper titled "Stochastic Differential-Cutoff Approximations for a Reversible Jumper Diffusion and Their Applications" built upon the previous work and found its own use in pricing options. A paper published in 2020 called "A Framework for Valuing Multi-Dimensional Time-Changing Volatility-Safe Options" continued this line of research. However, a 2021 publication called "A Framework for Valuing Time-Changing Volatility-Safe Options" revealed a mistake in the framework, which was corrected in the 2022 paper "Correcting the framework for the time-changing volatility-safe lemma". This final paper also successfully applied the correction by demonstrating how the corrected framework could be used to solve a path-dependent PDE for which Cai, Song and Kou's framework had failed. Furthermore, a method for approximating jump diffusions, developed by Song, Wang and Kou in 2020 for discrete time, was revealed to be itself flawed in 2022, leading to a corrected method for the partial distribution of a jump diffusion that same year. This document will summarize the contributions from the 2022 correction papers, first focusing on the framework, followed on the approximation. Interestingly, both papers revealed that the mistake in the framework, along with the flaw in the approximation, both arose from the failure to invert the covariance matrix $A^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A$ in the correct order. While this presents a significant challenge for the case of pricing options, it can be easily overcome for the case of approximations. We will also provide some potential solutions to these issues. Lastly, this document with conclude with some general thoughts on the value of inter-disciplinary mathematical collaboration.

Interpreting the inner workings of the complex, deep structure of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) continues to be a major goal in the field. However, due to its intricate nature, it is extremely difficult to understand the mechanisms at play. Research has identified the key components that drive decision-making in CNNs, particularly in classification tasks, via a hidden unit-based approach that provides an attention mechanism. Building on this existing research, we have expanded upon this idea by exploring the visual influences that lead to classification in CNNs. Our proposed approach, Hidden Visual-Semantic Filter Attention (HVSA), takes into account the interplay between a hidden layer and input activations, while also considering the semantic connection that exists. By achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets and providing a 93.22% accuracy on ImageNet, our method has significantly surpassed existing baseline techniques. Notably, our analysis of the results has revealed new insights, such as the diverse nature of decision-making, the reduction in feature ambiguity, and the significant role of semantic influence. The proposed HVSA approach and resulting results are now available on our GitHub page. We hope this research will help to advance the understanding and development of visual CNNs. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/aidg/Hidden-Visual-Semantic-Filter-Attention. The related paper has been published in the CALDAGRAMM 2021 proceedings. A more in-depth analysis has been shared in the CALDAGRAMM 2021 workshop. For any further inquiries, please feel free to reach out to deepai.guru@gmail.com. Our understanding of the results has been enhanced through the creation of in-depth, interactive visualizations (https://deepai-guru.github.io/hidden-visual-filter-attention/). Furthermore, we have added new interpretations, such as examining the decision-making process on CIFAR-10 using network structure from the widely used PyTorch library (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/main/torch/nn/modules/functional.py). The related Max Margin Classification (MMC) library has been hosted at https://github.com/andreou-max-m-margin-classification. We have also been working on creating a new neural attention-based approach, called Visual Explainer (https://github.com/DeepAIguru/Visual-Xplainer). By measuring how lattice vibrations impact the energy levels of these interactions, researchers evaluated the role of these vibrations in guiding copper's motion. Lattice vibrations significantly reduced the energy required for copper atoms to move towards each other, indicating that these vibrations facilitate attraction between them. In fact, for distances over six times the size of an atom, repulsive forces became attractive influences, with a significant decrease in energy by up to thirty times. This substantial modification to the energy levels shows that lattice vibrations have a profound impact on guiding copper's motion. Moreover, at certain temperatures, cuprate chains become more susceptible to a phase transition in which the movement of copper atoms becomes ordered. In fact, this susceptibility exists across a wider temperature range in one-dimensionally structured cuprate films compared to when they are grown on a flat surface. Therefore, researchers conclude that lattice vibrations play a pivotal role in guiding copper's motion in these materials. Further, when copper atoms move in tandem, the energy required for this movement increases in a specific, exponential manner with respect to distance, which is consistent with our earlier observations. In fact, this increase in energy, with a particular exponent, becomes more pronounced at higher temperatures in one-dimensionally structured cuprate film chains. In contrast, this phenomenon presents an intriguing contradiction when compared to when these materials are grown on a flat surface. To grasp intricate dynamic patterns between numerous time series, advanced statistical and machine learning models have been created to uncover the underlying causes. High-dimensional systems, where many time series often feature a large number of variables, pose significant challenges that certain models address directly. This research outlines and compares various methods for extracting hidden dynamics and measuring the hidden connections between these systems in high dimensions. These include multivariate extensions of the Elbow method, nonconvex optimization, and statistical tests for non-Gaussian high-dimensional time series. They are used to investigate a system driven by a few key variables and identify hidden patterns within real-world data, a cerebellar function monitoring system. This research discusses the successes and difficulties of the methods, highlighting their performance in accurately detecting the driving variables and measuring the temporal associations. The methods show great promise, particularly in low-dimensional systems, while facing precision issues and misinterpretation of noise as driving variables in high dimensions. Possible solutions and future research directions are explored, such as incorporating system sparsity and utilizing synthetic data generation to address these limitations. This research aims to provide in-depth, accessible explanations of these methods, ultimately aiming to facilitate their adoption by statisticians, biologists, and other related experts. They discuss the practical applications and potential modifications of these algorithms, many of which have not been widely available in the literature. The research also outlines several areas for further exploration, such as the use of Lagrangian optimization to promote system sparsity and the importance of error limits when testing for non-Gaussian time series. The supporting software and data for our findings have been made publicly available at https://github.com/duduchamp/highDimInfluence. Several years after the initial presentation, some of these algorithms have already been used in published research, such as the Elbow method, which was later known as "Structural Elbow" and applied to the analysis of EEG measurements in a research published in 2020, as well as the nonconvex optimization-based method, whose findings were published in a 2021 research using functional magnetic resonance imaging measurements. These algorithms' success demonstrate their potential to uncover the hidden patterns within high-dimensional systems. The research was partially completed while the author held a visiting researcher position at the University of California, Berkeley. We explore an extension of balance conditions applied to random functions or processes. A random variable is considered balanced if the expected value of its product with any linear functional is zero. This work assesses various properties of balanced random variables or their counterparts, estimated in sample balance, or derived using statistical balance techniques. A different approach to random variables, which we call stable points, can also be used to describe balance conditions. A stable point of a random variable is characterized as having an expected value that remains unchanged after applying any linear functional. We introduce a random stable point that satisfies specific conditions and can be used to recreate any random variable through a specific mathematical transformation. A distinct scenario is represented by balance problems of statistical physics, which we also explore. By applying our methods to solve the Navier-Stokes balance problem under certain conditions, we achieve results that demonstrate the existence of solutions to balance equations. A significant aspect of our approach involves estimating the degree of balance, which we calculate based on the coefficients of the Navier-Stokes equations or the matrix Porter-Thomas, which describes the rotation number in a quantum chaotic environment. Our approach offers a practical advantage, as it allows us to achieve balance in systems with or without bias, using or excluding rotation cycles. A corresponding algorithm has been developed and implemented in the Python programming language to solve the balance problem with stable points. A unique feature of our approach is the ability to create a balance transformation for finite probability spaces as well as random variables defined on arbitrary probability measures. We analyze the theoretical properties of the transformation, which we apply to a set of examples, including uniform, normal, and Stekowski distributions. Our results have been verified through numerical simulations."

Our approach leverages the latest developments in reliable neural networks, specifically in the fields of information-theoretic reversible processing and deeply conservative neural networks. We apply this concept to the realm of image authentication and forgery detection, using a method that treats genuine images as the preferred outcome. We develop a highly reliable authentication system, combining a polytomous reliable autoencoder and a new universal decoding algorithm. The proposed method significantly improves the overall performance compared to existing non-reversible techniques. The results of our experiments using NIST datasets reveal a substantial increase of 11-19% in classification accuracy over conventional methods, along with a substantial reduction of 2-4% in the false positive rate. Moreover, our proposed framework enables efficient detection and localization of forged areas. We compared the performance of universal decoders and found that the ones based on deeply conservative networks and information-theoretic reversible processing yield the best outcomes. We applied a similar framework to the task of forgery detection, using a different type of reliable authentication scheme - the point-wise reliable transformation. The ability to accurately detect and localize forged areas is achieved through the use of a mask prediction module. We tested our method using NIST datasets and found that it achieves a high overall accuracy of 90-95%, with the ability to accurately localize forged areas 97% of the time. Our proposed framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods of forgery detection in terms of accuracy and robust feature localization. We compared the performance of different reliable transformation types and found that the proposed point-wise approach surpasses others, particularly when evaluating the precision of detected forged areas. We introduced a new quality assessment method for neural networks, using a combination of reliable network properties and entropy to effectively measure the conceptuality of neural network layers. We applied this measure to authenticate images and found that it effectively links the level of data manipulation to the corresponding transformation's conceptuality. We tested our approach using NIST datasets and found that it achieves a high overall accuracy of 90-95%, with the ability to effectively measure the conceptuality of neural network layers 80% of the time. Our proposed framework outperforms existing state-of-art methods of neural network quality assessment. By accounting for all active helicities in mean-field frameworks, simulations demonstrate a notable improvement in reproducing dynamo performance across various regimes.  Furthermore, incorporating non-local and time-dependent turbulent influences proves to be essential for simulating dynamos to accurately produce magnetic energy. A simplified, test-particle-free solver for complex magnetic diffusion in plasmas uses a reduced kinetic model based on a generalized diffusion equation. This flexible framework can simulate various particle behaviors across different energy levels and collision types by adjusting kinetic coefficients. These coefficients calculate particle distribution via the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation, solving for a reduced particle density and its associated currents. This discussion will focus on a numerical method for solving the generalized diffusion equation, incorporating spatial and temporal diffusion, as well as collision processes with a fixed point in space. An finite element method is used for spatial solution, coupled with a semi-implicit time-stepping approach that maintains solution conservation. This conservative approach enables accurate simulation of system dynamics without time-driven errors. This method effectively calculates key parameters such as the plasma's thermal force, drag, and inertial force, preserving global mass and energy balance. An example simulation demonstrates the method's conservation properties. Furthermore, we investigate the numerical solution's convergence using both theoretical and practical methods, deriving a convergence rate for the finite element method as initially proven for conservative magnetic diffusion equations. An example simulation demonstrates the method's convergence by showing a $|u_h|_{\partial t}$ ratio that converges towards zero with a specified time step, using the Schwinger function as an energy metric. Last, we validate the method through an example simulation of a particle experiencing both thermal force and drag in a fixed, horizontal magnetic field. This test shows a steady-state particle balance that would occur in a perfect conductor. The method's code has also been optimized for use in a particle-transport code called AVALON. An example simulation from this code demonstrates the method's effectiveness in tracking particle migration across a variety of complex magnetic fields. An example simulation reveals that in a particle, the lateral diffusion may significantly exceed the longitudinal diffusion. This ratio exceeds 100 when the particle's energy is equal to the thermal energy of its surrounding plasma. This outcome confirms a well-known principle and also highlights the effectiveness of this method's optimization for use in various kinetic models. The code's performance has also been validated for equal diffusion in both lateral and longitudinal directions. This code has also been shown to perfectly conserve key parameters in a test simulation, consistent with the underlying physics of perfect conductors. The code also shows a specified convergence rate in a test simulation, consistent with the underlying kinetic theory. We have now successfully adapted and implemented these methods on standard continuous problems. Efforts were made to evaluate the consistency of variable stepsize SDGIMs, which was already known for constant step sizes. However, attempts to establish convergence at a rate of p with adaptive time steps resulted in failures for p greater than one. Therefore, this study further developed and tested SDGIMs on standard continuous problems to investigate the performance of these methods under various time step strategies. Moreover, numerical experiments were carried out to assess the efficiency of these methods. The results revealed that variable stepsize SDGIMs outperform those with constant step sizes in terms of accuracy while enhancing computational efficiency. Notably, these methods have the potential to compete with Nordsieck-based SDGIMs in terms of overall performance. Furthermore, theoretical error estimates were established and analyzed. The results showed that variable stepsize SDGIMs can achieve a level of accuracy comparable to theoretical predictions. Consequently, these methods have the potential to be adopted as reliable numerical tools for solving continuous problems in the future. Alternatively, users can input the energy levels and quantum numbers to graph the corresponding substance's radial density distribution. The associated neutral hydrogen gas within low-mass galaxies plays a significant role due to their increased interaction with the cosmic microwave background radiation, making them suitable objects to study early universe processes. A key factor affecting early universe predictions comes from high-redshift dwarf galaxies, but finding counterparts at those redshifts is nearly impossible. A more feasible option is to analyze dwarf galaxies nearby that have similar gas metabolism to their higher-redshift counterparts. By examining the gas metabolism rates of nearby dwarf galaxies, researchers can place constraints on cosmic baryon flow, influencing the predicted characteristics of high-redshift galaxies. In this review, we will analyze the gas metabolism of nearby dwarf galaxies to predict the scale of cosmic baryon flow, before comparing it to observations of more distant galaxies. In addition, we will discuss potential star formation rates in dwarf galaxies and the impact of their outflowing gases, highlighting the need for further detection of these outflowing gases at various redshifts. A potential tool in this pursuit is the study of X-ray detection of outflowing gases in galaxies, a method proven effective through its application in the galaxy M33. However, a major challenge remains the detection of outflowing gases through absorption features at ultraviolet wavelengths. A recent study analyzed the absorption features in 65 different galaxies, but was limited by its small sample size. A more comprehensive study incorporating the samples of multiple, high-star-producing galaxies is required to accurately analyze the gas metabolism of galaxies. Such a study could have significant implications, including the understanding of the role early outflowing gases play in the development of their more massive, star-producing galaxy counterparts. Furthermore, further research into the gas metabolism of galaxies could also shed light on the development of galaxies with little to no existing stellar mass. Notably, a recent study discovered high-velocity outflowing gases in a massive dwarf galaxy. Text-video retrieval has gained significant popularity due to the surge in demand for video search. The main obstacle is to address the gap between text and video modalities by learning a common cross-modal space. Current top-ranking methods use a cross-attention mechanism to match tokens from text and video features. However, they face challenges with capturing the overall meaning of single tokens and suffer from feature embedding bias. To overcome these issues, we present a new architecture called TS2-Net, which includes two key innovations. Firstly, we introduce a token shift operator to produce features from different spatial or temporal tokens within a single frame. This allows single tokens to capture broader content and improves overall cross-modal representation. Secondly, we develop a token choice mechanism to select the most relevant feature from each modality for final prediction. Experimental evaluations on various public datasets reveal that TS2-Net has achieved remarkable performance with significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art retrieval models. Specifically, it achieves an accuracy of 75.8% for Kiwi, 83.8% for VATEX, and 75.4% for ActivityNet, surpassing 13 top-ranked baselines by a large margin. Notably, it surpasses the second-best model, I3S, in all cases without employing a separate transformer for video framing. Moreover, TS2-Net achieves superior performance while using a much smaller model, consisting of only 25M parameters, making it extremely efficient, processing video at a rate of 30fps. In this study, we propose a novel framework that allows us to develop novel GP kernels by combining fundamental expressions. Our research shows that by forming a graph from a kernel's expression, we can utilize graph-based methods to identify similar kernels. In addition to this, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on several significant real-world tasks, such as modeling the effects of drugs on cells and predicting minicut times in autonomous driving scenarios. Our results suggest that by graph-based kernel engineering, we can efficiently create GP models capable of addressing complex challenges with limited resources. The framework itself, along with our findings, have been made publicly accessible at a dedicated webpage. It can also be found within the open-source Python library known as PyGPKernel, which was utilized in our study.

Traditional methods for training neural networks to discard irrelevant information relied on fixed 'pruning' patterns, strictly adhering to pre-defined sparsity profiles. In contrast, we present 'Spartan', a groundbreaking differentiable technique enabling a more adaptive, error-correcting approach. By seamlessly integrating dropout and l1 regularization, we formulate a unique 'conveyance' term that efficiently regulates neural sparsity. Our evaluations demonstrate Spartan on various tasks - including visual classification using ResNet, and word-level language modeling with LSTM - show it can not only mimic the sparsity achieved with conventional methods but also outperform them significantly, achieving improved results with enhanced efficiency. Furthermore, we show Spartan effectively reduces the computational and memory burdens associated with large, modern neural networks. Ultimately, we examine Spartan's applicability to a broad spectrum of tasks and discuss the implications for efficient neural architecture design. The Spartan code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexmapes/spartan. Videos illustrating the method can be viewed at https://dr.com/spartan.

In systems with vortices, the presence of vorticity often leads to the appearance of the Berthelot phenomenon, a phenomenon characterized by the intermixing of vortices of differing topological properties, which results in the emergence of new vortical structures separated by irregular interfaces.  Within the context of this process, we investigate a unique phenomenon in which vortices with unitary properties merge with their opposites, giving rise to homogeneous vortical states within previously untopological regions. Our investigation focuses on a Bose fluid characterized by weakly interacting atoms. Rather than employing a particle-by-particle analysis, we use a macroscopic approach, thereby leveraging the extensive statistical weight associated with these systems to identify an unusual constraint preventing the homogeneous expansion of vortices. Upon determining that this constraint can indeed influence the behavior of vortices, we turn our attention to a related question: what safeguards protect the extensive statistical weight associated with vortices from erosion? Our analysis reveals that a unique quantum-related constraint, stemming from the absence of interactions between vortices in the far distance, comes to play a critical role, and we derive this constraint through a novel calculation. Our investigation provides new insights into the characteristics of weakly interacting Bose fluids at low temperatures, and it could potentially be replicated using advanced magnetic levitation technology. Moreover, our findings highlight the intricate interconnectedness between statistical mechanics and the quantum properties of matter, providing a fresh perspective on the study of vortical structures within quantum systems. Finally, we note that a unique constraint preventing the fusion of vortices is not the sole example of an unusual constraint within the realm of statistical mechanics, and we discuss the broader implications of this phenomenon. Nevertheless, despite our ability to identify this constraint, we demonstrate that it is not applicable in cases involving strongly interacting vortices, and we illustrate this point using the example of a Bose fluid characterized by strongly interacting atoms. Our investigation provides a fresh perspective on the study of vortical structures within quantum systems, and it could potentially inspire future research into the intricate world of statistical mechanics and quantum physics. Moreover, our work introduces a novel concept, referred to as the emergent Pauli obstruction, which may be applied to a broad range of quantum systems, including superconductors and superfluids characterized by zero chemical potential. The concept is based on a unique constraint requiring the homogeneity of vortices within untopological regions, and it could be used to develop a variety of statistical mechanics-based constraints in the future. Previous researchers discovered that a small percentage of faulty codes with compilation issues are often referred to as'stinkers', and further study indicated that these codes tend to recur. 
In this study, developers linked predisposition to coding errors and their likelihood of occurrence. 
Empirical studies conducted with 504 developers provided the context in which'stinker' characteristics and their frequency are viewed by the developers. 
It was noted that some factors contributing to coding errors are universally agreed upon by developers while opinions may vary on others. 
 In addition, our studies show that developers universally agree on the frequency of some coding errors while have differing opinions on the frequency of others. 
In light of these findings, the possibility of mitigating'stinker' characteristics is explored. 

Researchers identified 32 universally agreed upon coding errors and 47 errors with varying levels of agreement. 
Non-recursive errors were agreed upon by 98\% of developers and ranked 16 out of 32. 
By contrast, non-null pointer errors at assignment were agreed upon by 61\% of developers and ranked 28 out of 47. 
It is worth noting that some errors with universal agreement were not observed frequently in real-world applications, indicating a potential gap between the perfect static analysis and actual code quality. 
Closing the gap would result in better code quality. 
In addition to improving static analyses, our findings suggest the need for educational efforts to increase awareness among developers regarding the frequency of coding errors.

This study presents a novel model named Tiramisu, which can quickly and accurately determine inter-beat intervals from raw electrocardiogram signals. Compared to existing methods, the Tiramisu model demonstrates enhanced efficacy with reduced error. Our technique is founded on two key concepts: the tensor singular value decomposition, and the singular value decomposition of a matrix. Depending on the need for speed or memory, our algorithm can be executed in either row-major or column-major order, making it suitable for both memory-constrained and speed-constrained scenarios. Our method incorporates an optional parameter that determines the number of passes, allowing the user to adjust computation time based on specific requirements. When the number of passes is set to the size of the tensor along a particular dimension, the algorithm will generate an accurate tenor decomposition, but this can be an impractically high number in many situations. As such, our method provides an effective trade-off between the quality of the solution and the time and space resources required to achieve it. Our method can be supplemented with an affordable supplemental pass that enhances the solution's accuracy if the additional resources are available. Our algorithm is predicated on two key theoretical postulates, and we have empirically validated the performance of this method through numerous tests. These tests involved determining the time and linear regression loss (a measure of accuracy) for various numbers of passes, and we found that our new technique compares favorably to another, non-stochastic method for approximating the t-SVD. Our research demonstrates that linear regression loss is inversely related to the number of passes, and that increasing the number of passes by a factor of ten reduces the linear regression loss by about the same amount. probability measures with small maxima and explore homological persistence as
a tool for detecting such structures. Notably, when the dimension of the
manifold increases relative to the data's dimension, a transition occurs where
Betti numbers' bimodality shifts from homological Betti numbers over synthetic
Betti numbers. Moreover, we establish the effect of increasing zeros on the
Betti numbers and show that, as the number of zeros in the model increases,
homological Betti numbers converge to those of a probability measure with no
manifold structure. Notably, when Gaussian data is corrupted with sparse noise
in high dimensions, a transitional regime occurs where meaningful patterns are
lost but still detectable with homological persistence. These results form
the foundation for a statistical inference framework, where principled selection
methods using homological persistence detect meaningful patterns in sparse
models, even when they diverge from the Gaussian distribution. Moreover, our
results highlight that homological persistence offers a natural, principled
method for identifying sparse structures in high-dimensional data. We apply
these techniques to data from the NIST Phase Retrieval Challenge. Assuming known
knowledge of zeros or using homological persistence to infer zeros, our
analysis demonstrates that sparse models can be applied even to data that is
not initially known to be marginally multivariate Gaussian. Importantly, our
patterns are confirmed to be stable across various homotopy transformations.

Typically, in reinforcement learning, a agent is taught to maximize its rewards with an undefined instructor in mind. In this study, the instructor's intentions are explicitly communicated through feedback and constraints that limit the possible actions and their effects. 

RCRT training utilises policy gradient optimization to discover an instructor model. This model mimics the instructor's thought process by simulating their strategy for issuing feedback and adjusting parameters when needed. 

To evaluate our approach, we trained a robot to perform vocational tasks. Our robot received feedback and task constraints during its training, allowing us to replicate the instructor's strategy. 

Moreover, by characterising the instructor's policy using dynamic programming, we verified the accuracy of our replica. Our experiments demonstrate that our replica accurately replicates the instructor's original policy, leading to better performance of the robot. This allows our agent to learn more effectively with the instructor's strategy as a guide. 

Our novel RCRT presents an original framework for learning the instructor's strategy. This framework can be adapted for diverse constrained reinforcement learning scenarios and serves as a potential template. Furthermore, our research explores applications of the instructor model, indicating additional benefits. One significant application of the instructor model is in transferring knowledge to alleviate the credit assignment problem. This is done by preserving constraints while allowing the agent to interpret the instructor's strategy freely. Another potential use of the instructor model is in enabling level design for games. This is done by allowing the instructor to adjust the game dynamics and reward structure during training to guide the agent towards desired outcomes.

We introduce OntoPlot, a novel visualisation for illustrating connections between entities within extensive, detailed knowledge frameworks. Differing from standard hierarchies, OntoPlot handles relationships between equal-rank objects by displaying them as radial links originating from a central point, representing'me too' interactions, where each connected entity represents an affirmation or association. To accommodate vast knowledge bases, we have refined OntoPlot's design to highlight and filter the numerous, intricate connections it contains. We have conducted comprehensive user testing on multiple versions of the plot and gathered user feedback to refine the design. Ultimately, we have implemented OntoPlot using D3 and demonstrated its capabilities with three substantial knowledge bases: Bibsonomy, DBpedia, and YAGO, all hierarchically organised yet featuring numerous'me too' interactions. By presenting OntoPlot, we aim to contribute a novel visualisation concept that can inspire similar designs for visualising complex, interacting connections within knowledge frameworks. Furthermore, the diverse applications of OntoPlot make it a versatile tool, capable of being easily integrated into a wide range of systems, including research tools, management platforms, and educational environments. You can access an interactive demonstration of OntoPlot at https://lilywangdo.github.io/OntoPlot-Website/. Similarly, we have generated artificial connection data for OntoPlot, to ensure that user interactions are not influenced by the actual structure of the DBpedia knowledge base. OntoPlot's website serves not only as an interactive platform for visualising the knowledge frameworks but also as a comprehensive resource providing information on these entities, including statistics and system integration instructions. Furthermore, the website includes a knowledge library where visitors can access various knowledge frameworks and learn how to incorporate them into their own custom visualisations. The design files for OntoPlot, as well as all of the data used to create the interactive visualisation, can be obtained from the website's resource section. By making these files freely accessible, we have enabled users to modify and contribute to the design, thereby expanding the capabilities of OntoPlot and creating new, innovative visualisation concepts that can be shared globally. Our method involves using CycleGAN to create noise maps in the same domain as the target speech, allowing for noise reduction through speaker normalization. The Proactive Active Inference Framework is a reliable method for guiding a robot's movement in unpredictable environments. Despite the absence of a predetermined map, our approach enables the robot to independently explore and reach its desired destination. The simplicity and adaptability of this theoretical framework make it a great choice for navigating complex and dynamic settings, as it doesn't require pre-mapped information. The theory for Soret effects in fluids with internal structures has been developed and applied across various systems to understand how temperature gradients affect migration within those fluids. However, the current framework is missing a crucial aspect - the influence of internal degrees of freedom on the Soret flow. To address this gap, a generalized framework is introduced, enabling the evaluation of Soret suction in fluids composed of soft molecules that can change shape. Focusing on poly2D and poly3D models, where soft molecules have two or three nematic degrees of freedom, the Soret suction is calculated for both stress-diffusion and rotationally invariant regimes. The results are presented as Valles-Beltrami modules that can be used to predict the Soret effect in systems with various internal degrees of freedom. The theory is particularly relevant to understanding Soret effects in proteins and peptides. Furthermore, to validate the developed framework, numerical simulations were conducted using both Brownian dynamics and Langevin dynamics for systems consisting of poly3D molecules, confirming the theory's predictions. The developed framework is expected to facilitate experimental research on Soret effects in fluids with internal structures. We introduce the Box re-Ranking (BRR) method, which employs online instance learning to eliminate false positives produced by modern pedestrian detectors. By reducing these false positives, BRR enhances the reliability of pedestrian detection while operating independently of the original detector's architecture. We utilize online instance learning via a simple, yet effective two-class classifier that performs self-supervision to minimize false positives. A key innovation of BRR lies in addressing the challenge of reducing false positives while preserving detection accuracy for actual pedestrians. To achieve this, we employ a straightforward yet critical online selection process that selects which false positives to eliminate. Experimental validation on the Citypersons and Citypersons+ benchmarks demonstrates a substantial reduction in false positives, with up to 43% fewer errors on more challenging datasets while still achieving high recall rates for actual pedestrians. Notably, BRR has been designed with a low computational overhead, enabling it to operate at a speed of 34.1 FPS on the Tesla K80 GPU. The source code for BRR will be publicly available. The success of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the use of binding energy values, yet experimentally determined values are scarce and simulation-based estimates vary greatly. To overcome this issue, a database of quantum chemical binding energy distributions has been developed and launched online for the astrochemical community to use. This new platform allows users to input specific molecule combinations and receive estimated dissociation energy values, based on extensive calculations by the research team. This approach offers advantages over traditional methods, offering results valid across a wide temperature range (10 K to 500 K) and preserving statistical error from molecular pair distributions. To facilitate further research, a related study has explored the general observability of simulated binding energy distributions, with findings that can be applied across various astrophysical and laboratory settings. This understanding is then used to develop a model for translating microstate distribution binding energies into observable line intensity profiles. This model shows great potential in helping researchers assess the feasibility of detecting specific molecular species in various astrophysical environments and laboratory experiments. By combining these approaches, a versatile tool for the astrochemical community has been developed to enable accurate and reliable estimates of binding energy values. This tool is available online at https://www.binding-energy.org. Furthermore, associated software repositories and demos can be accessed at https://github.com/bill-wark/AstroBED. This research has been published in a paper titled "The Binding Energy Assessment Platform (AstroBED): A database of quantum chemical binding energy distributions for the astrochemical community," which is accessible at 10.5194/a&a-2022-10. Our related software package "bedplus" is available at https://github.com/bill-wark/bedplus. This software enables users to either extend existing binding energy distributions or use existing bed+ objects to calculate simulated binding energy distributions. We introduce a technique for estimating the average value of a given operator $O$ within a low-energy state $ |psi$ created by a short, random Clifford circuit acting on $N$ qubits. Our approach relies on a random sampling of $M$ distinct states $ |psi_f$ that are relatively close to $ |psi$. Notably, the proposed scheme is efficient for $M$ when considering the total number of possible states, but it does so by drawing from this vast set in a non-adaptive manner. Building on this concept, we explore applying this technique to specific scenarios, such as diagnosing whether a particular state is in a familiar form or estimating the fidelity of a given state. Our results suggest that this approach can be highly resilient to variations even in cases where perfect performance isn't attained. Our findings provide the foundation for further research into non-adaptive sampling methods that may offer more prospects for beating the limitations imposed by the vast complexity of quantum many-body states. Our code for this project has been made available. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our shallow-shades approach can also be applied by performing experiments on a 5-qubit NISQ device to accurately assess the inner state of a freestyle qubit. This experiment showcases the potential real-world applications of our technique. Our experiment design is detailed in the paper. The project's code can also be found at this GitHub link: https://github.com/McMinerva/shallow-shades/tree/main/src/shallow-shades.py. For instance, to accurately determine the expectation value of $(X_1 \dots X_n)^2$ for a state $ |psi$, our method successfully achieved precision within $10^{-6}$ of the known accurate result, using just a single experiment with a 5-qubit NISQ device and without any post-processing of the raw data. This outcome significantly surpasses the device's native precision of around $10^{-4}$. Our experiments indicate that this effect stems from the production of shades that are rotationally aligned. Our results demonstrate that this approach can be highly effective even in cases where the shades aren't densely packed. Our experiments provide the foundation for further research into universal estimation for general observables. Notably, a key benefit of transfer learning involves enhancing the performance of a model on a target task by training it on a related, but disparate, dataset. However, implementing transfer learning requires the identification of a suitable source dataset that is essentially representative of the target task. To overcome this challenge, researchers have lately proposed a new class of transfer learning approaches, where a source dataset is created synthetically, using datasets from unrelated tasks. By generating source datasets in this manner, they can be assured to be "informative" in relation to the target task, thereby ensuring that a source dataset with a high degree of transferability can be identified. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of a dataset with high informativity for any given polylinear illustration. Utilizing multilingual language models can be beneficial in numerous low-resource settings, such as language detection, detection of fake news and zero-shot translation. Nonetheless, deploying such models inside mobile devices' limited RAM is impractical through conventional approaches. We investigate two potential methods for reducing the memory footprint of these models: quantization and word extraction. We analyze their resilience using various models and word extraction techniques and evaluate their translated outputs with metrics like BLEU scores. We discover that either method is capable of significantly decreasing a model's memory requirements while preserving its effectiveness, with gains of up to 75% over baseline models given a fixed context window size. Furthermore, we find that both methods are applicable to a broad spectrum of pre-trained models, including those based on ALBERT, BERT and RoBERTa, providing a flexible framework for model optimization. We ultimately develop a set of optimized word extraction models, weighing approximately 43.64 megabytes, tailored for mobile speech translation applications. We validate these models through a speech translation task and find they significantly outperform the baseline model, achieving a 16.7 vs 4.9 BLEU score difference on EN-ES translation. The code for this research will be publicly accessible via GitHub. We hope our study will contribute to developing lightweight low-resource MT models. We also aim to make these models accessible to users on mobile devices and other restricted platforms. We will present our research at WMT2022 and submit our extracted models to the IJCNLP-2022, where they will compete in the WINMT-2022, LIAM at IJCNLP-2022 contest. The analysis leading up to our work reveals that for the segmentation of pneumonia areas within chest X-rays, using enhanced images is beneficial even when only labeled for normal lung areas. This is because the task becomes achievable by enhancing the image to make pneumonia lesions more distinguishable than normal lung tissue. To confirm this, we developed an image enhancement technique grounded in pixel class probabilities that doesn't demand complex computational power, and we tested its effectiveness on both the private hospital's dataset and public Jockey dataset. By utilizing our proposed method, the best public dataset accuracy achieved an 82.14% improvement, and similarly, the accuracy on our private hospital's dataset saw an 84.29% improvement. Furthermore, this methodology has the added advantage of reducing the quantity of labeled data needed, and it doesn't affect the way images are pre-processed in the typical manner. As a result, even with normal lung labels, our proposed method facilitates accurate pneumonia lesion segmentation. This method is now being used in an ongoing clinical study at the private hospital to automatically identify pneumonia cases. Following further refinement, the goal is to apply this automated system widely in other healthcare establishments. A GitHub repository has been created with the proposed code and datasets to facilitate reproducibility. Recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs) have led to remarkable results in various natural language processing tasks through the use of pre-training and fine-tuning. However, giving explanations and understanding the reasoning behind LLMs' outputs remains a significant challenge. This study presents a novel approach to generate images descriptions via LLMs without the need for explicit training on the task. We employ a prompt engineering technique, dividing it into off-training and inference time, to fine-tune a GPT2 LLM to generate descriptions for image embeddings. We evaluate our approach on the Conceptual Captions dataset and compare its performance with state-of-the-art image description models. The results demonstrate that our method produces high-quality descriptions, surpassing other techniques in both coherence and accuracy. Notably, our approach's descriptions reveal a more predictable set of concepts, highlighting their utility in model evaluation and prompt analysis. This study also explores the effect of varying prompts and demonstrates its adaptability to different A/B testing scenarios for prompt optimization. We propose using unlabelled data to optimize image description prompts during inference time, leading to significant improvements in coherence and accuracy. We make our code and pre-trained models available for further research. Overall, our study contributes to the development of regulatable image description models via prompt engineering, paving the way for the creation of explainable language models. We discuss potential applications and extend this research to other image processing tasks, promoting the development of prompt-based techniques. Finally, we outline avenues for future research and make the related project available at https://github.com/sudhanshusharma/image-description-prompt-engineering.

Our research introduces zero-shot voice translation, which enables translation without language overlap using utterance-level acoustic features as input signals. We develop a neural model that combines a speaker-independent synthesis system with a neural transcription model and a neural translation model. To achieve this, we rely on the existing AST (artery-speech-transcript) dataset to bypass transcription during data collection, allowing for the creation of a single, end-to-end model. Through model selection and performance evaluation, we demonstrate that our approach can achieve comparable results to state-of-the-art speech-to-text models on three public datasets, including Librispeech and the NIST CSLU08, NIST CSLU10 Arabic datasets, through either 50% fewer parameters or increased data augmentation. To the best knowledge, this, our voice translation model is the first to operate without requiring prior knowledge of the spoken language and without overlapping translation languages. Furthermore, it can translate spoken material by listening to speech waves. We also showcase our approach by successfully translating dialogues from English to Mandarin, which is notoriously difficult for machine translation. We anticipate that our work will open a new avenue for cross-language speech translation in the future. The general theory involves boundary terms with complex evolution, followed by an in-depth examination of more practical situations, including processes restricted within an enclosed space with variable boundary areas. The study also covers situations where heat can escape but not enter, and scenarios where heat generation and loss are equal, and we investigate the long-term behavior of these systems. The methods employed for analysis and proof are from the theory of monotone operators and the properties of accretive operators. The discussion is supplemented by examples and a concrete model of heat transfer involving a solid with boundaries subject to different temperature-dependent cooling rules. One potential solution could be the combination of short-term and long-term forecasts. While short-term forecasts, based on recent data, might be precise yet uncertain and unreliable, long-term forecasts, based on comprehensive information but weak in precision, can provide a degree of reliability. In this research, we study the potential benefits of merging these forecasts with a stochastic approach. Furthermore, we explore how incorporating the predicted daily peak load into the forecast fusion model can contribute to optimized forecast performance. In our experiments, the application of mCGAN, a category-generated adversarial network, alongside traditional ARIMA and RFR forecasting methods demonstrated improved results when incorporating daily peak forecasts. Notably, this improvement persisted even when only relying on long-term forecasts. Nevertheless, the mCGAN model failed to surpass the performance of conventional methods when working alone. Nonetheless, as part of a hybrid forecasting system, mCGAN could be a valuable addition. Further studies are needed to assess the real-life practicality of incorporating daily peak forecasts in real-world settings. One possible limitation could be the additional uncertainty introduced when transmitting and receiving daily peak profiles. In order to minimize this extra uncertainty, it may be necessary to significantly enhance the signal strength of these profiles, perhaps by collecting more data points. The integration of domain expertise in machine learning is a critical challenge that needs to be addressed to ensure the quality of learning systems. We begin by identifying the core issues surrounding domain expertise in machine learning and outlining a framework to incorporate this domain expertise at various stages within a machine learning pipeline. By providing a general method for incorporating domain expertise, we can apply it to multiple settings, such as modifying loss functions or using learning algorithms that incorporate domain knowledge. We illustrate the practical application of this integration in knowledge graph learning, specifically through the use of semantic embeddings. 

Keywords: domain expertise integration, machine learning, knowledge graph learning, semantic embeddings.

In the field of chest CT analysis for COVID-19, researchers face a significant obstacle due to the disease's variable manifestations and hidden lesions. The typical approach relies on collecting anchor boxes and conducting box-refinement to produce predictable results. Nevertheless, this strategy's reliance on box quality to determine segmentation accuracy can be problematic when dealing with COVID-19. To address this limitation, a more efficient method called Weakly Guided Learning (WGL) is explored in this study. By integrating pandemic-related prior knowledge and leveraging noise-sensitive distribution alignment, the proposed framework enhances lesion detection and reduces reliance on box quality. The approach, named WWNet, was evaluated using the COVID19-CT dataset and outperformed conventional anchors and refinement techniques by significant margins, specifically demonstrating an average Hausdorff distance of $0.45\pm0.06$ millimeters and $2.14\pm0.66$ percent change in Dice score compared to other methods. Furthermore, WWNet's improved lesion detection capabilities and segmentation precision led to higher accuracy in diagnostic feature extraction, with a significant $4.22\pm0.63$ percent increase in dice score compared to other methods. Vertebral bodies are critical to spine health and their accurate analysis through radiological imaging can provide valuable insights into musculoskeletal conditions. However, the automation of vertebral localization and recognition in CT scans remains a challenging task, largely due to common spine pathologies and the lack of distinctive features in normal vertebras. To overcome these difficulties, a novel approach has been developed based on distinguishing vertebas by analyzing their characteristics in the sagittal plane and optimizing their positions in the coronal plane in line with normal vertebras' patterns. The process involves correcting potential spine distortions through spine rectification techniques. The efficacy of the approach has been tested using CT scans with or without vertebral implants and the results show promising accuracy of vertebral body recognition. The method has been successfully applied to recognize and localize vertebras in CT scans with cervical, thoracic and lumbar regions combined. The accuracy of the approach has been confirmed through extensive testing on 330 CT volumes. The accuracy of vertebral body recognition ranged from 99.7% to 99.9% and the accuracy of localization ranged from 98.9% to 99.2%. The integration of the approach with other technologies, such as robotic systems, could provide significant value in clinical settings. The approach has been released as an open-source software called SpineLocOR for further development and use by other researchers. The information on CT scans, the approach's design and the evaluation results are provided in the paper. The provided slides summarize the key findings from the study. A key aspect of quantum theory is its ability to distinguish between various internal states of systems. However, when only observational data is considered without accounting for influences like decoherence, deciding the actual state of a system can be challenging. This difficulty arises from the fact that two mutually exclusive hypotheses may lead to indistinguishable experimental results, rendering the state selection process uncertain. A new approach, inspired by the quantum Radon inverse problem, proposes to resolve this indeterminacy by forming a set of feasible states, all of which align with observed data. This method then utilizes measures such as the mutual information or the trace distance to quantify the state's uniqueness. It is demonstrated that these measures remain non-degenerate provided the state's fiducial margin remains substantial. This indeterminacy threshold, referred to as the fiducial boundary, marks the point at which state uniqueness becomes certain. An investigation into the characteristics of this boundary reveals that it emerges in a symmetric manner around the state's angular direction. Furthermore, it has a convex shape and remains bounded from both sides. This method can also be used to determine the precise time when state degeneracy occurs under laboratory conditions where two states evolve according to different Hamiltonians. As an example, it is shown that when state degeneracy occurs, it will be the point in time when the trace of the commutator between the state's decay rates and the evolving Hamiltonian will become zero. This research demonstrates that quantum state evolution is a method to distinguish between quantum states that are becoming identical but have different evolutionary paths. This approach to the quantum state distinguishability issue can be applied not only to individual systems, but also to the interaction and co-evolution of multiple systems based on joint observational data. In the realm of fashion, where images are frequently utilized, developing algorithms to modify image attributes becomes a significant concern. This challenge is particularly demanding when dealing with retrieval tasks, as existing images are frequently abundant but control over their attributes is limited. This study presents a semi-supervised method to address this issue. By employing a supervised approach, our method aims to identify the dress style from a given image and then modifies the target image feature by incorporating the identified dress style through a matching network. This approach is then combined with an unsupervised attribute editor to refine the manipulation results. By editing feature-level traits in fashion images, our method enhances the accuracy of retrieval algorithms, ultimately allowing users to obtain more accurate results with less original image content. Experimental validation of our method on two fashion datasets demonstrates its superiority over existing algorithms in terms of retrieving relevant images.
