The Mathematician Hadamard developed the concept of stability in models in the early 20th century and identified certain integral kernels to be unambiguous within the context of Hilbert spaces; however, these concepts did not extend to general vector spaces. To address this limitation, a mathematical framework was introduced by a 2018 paper, which provided methods for ill-posed problems within the context of Hilbert spaces. In an effort to extend this work, we present a new algorithm that operates independently of specific space structures by introducing a dual gradient descent method. Furthermore, we provide examples of well-posedness and existence for ill-posed problems in both Banach and Hilbert spaces. Lastly, we illustrate the performance of the dual gradient descent method using numerical experiments based on two real-world applications: electron tomography and electrostatic backprojection. By implementing the former algorithm for these applications, we demonstrate that the dual gradient descent method surpasses its predecessors in efficiency. Consequently, our results establish a direct extension of Hadamard's findings in the context of vector spaces. The methods presented here are implemented in the 'penSpace' Python package, which is publicly available via GitHub. The package also includes a variety of generalizations of the algorithms introduced in the 2018 paper. The 'penSpace' package can be accessed via: https://github.com/Stratanovici/penSpace. The numerical experiments were conducted using the 'tomPy' Python package, which is available at: https://github.com/Stratanovici/tomPy. The tomPy package serves as the tomography module of penSpace and is responsible for handling the algorithms within the 'Applications': submodule. Furthermore, the nonconvex optimization module, the'stranOpt' module was incorporated, which is available at: https://github.com/Stratanovici/stranOpt. The numerical experiments presented in the thesis represent a synthesis of the author's undergraduate research project at the University of Regina, which was supervised by penSpace's developer. A novel, deep learning-based approach has been developed for light field depth estimation through parameter optimization. The solution employs a flexible, data-driven model that captures the intrinsic and extrinsic characteristics of each view. Unlike existing methods, our approach effectively handles occlusions by assigning meaningful values to missing pixels in each view. As a result, it can accurately detect even heavily occluded regions. Evaluation on rigorous, artificial 7x7 arrays and challenging natural 3D scenes with significant occlusions surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art solutions, even when incorporating results from state-of-the-art depth estimation methods. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/husseinHakeem/MLProjects/tree/main/OcclusionAwareLFDE. The light field datasets can be accessed at https://sites.google.com/view/linglinghan/home. The center-slice light field array dataset is available at https://github.com/maseo-san/CenterSliceLightFieldArrayDataset. The center slice array dataset on GitHub does not contain the actual arrays, but it includes a Python script to generate them. The code was tested using Python 3.9.5 and PyTorch 1.12.1. The repository contains the code for the approach as well as the data used in the evaluation, including artificial arrays and the dataset on GitHub called "dior Rose". The evaluation was performed without any modifications to the code. The artificial arrays and the dataset on GitHub called "dior Rose" were both used as input to assess the approach. The approach was tested with fixed camera parameters across all views. The parameter 'epsilon' in the loss function was set to 0.05. The approach was trained in batches of 32. The number of epochs was set to 200. The approach achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.21 when trained without prior depth estimates. When combined with prior depth estimates, the MAE reduced to 0.15. When prior depth estimates are unavailable, the approach achieves a pixel accuracy (PA) of 0.5868. By incorporating existing depth estimates, the PA increases to 0.7139. For the approach to maintain its performance on natural scenes, it is recommended to apply post-processing techniques such as median filtering. A detailed description of the approach and evaluation is provided in the main document. The source code and datasets are provided as per the repository structure. The solution has been successfully demonstrated through a video available at https://github.com/husseinHakeem
